speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1.	His Majesty has appointed a minister at Washington, with the special object of representing in the United States of America the interests of the Dominion of Canada. The minister will present his credentials to the President of the United States on February 18. Provision for the expenses of the legation was made in the estimates of 1926-27, and further provision will be included in the estimates for 1927-28, which will shortly be laid before parliament.
2.	The staff will probably consist of two first secretaries, a commercial secretary, a private secretary, and four clerks and stenographers.
3.	Hon. Yincent Massey has been appointed as minister, during His Majesty's pleasure. His salary will be $12,000 a year; house and representation allowance has not yet been definitely set. His title is "His Britannic Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary at Washington to represent the interests of the Dominion of Canada," or briefly, "the Canadian minister to the United States."
4.	No. Parliament has repeatedly considered the principle of special Canadian representation in the United States. On May 10, 1920, the Acting Prime Minister, Sir George Foster, announced in the House of Commons that "as a result of recent discussion an arrangement has been concluded between the British and Canadian governments to provide more complete representation of Canadian interests than has hitherto existed." On April 21, 1921, in committee of supply, during a discussion of an appropriation for Canadian representation in the
United States, Sir Robert Borden gave a comprehensive survey of the development of opinion and policy on this question from 1870 to 1921. Provision for the expenses of such Canadian representation has been included in the estimates each year since and including 1919-20, and approved in all ,cases by parliament.
5.	The minister will be charged with the duty of advancing the interests of Canada in the United States and will serve as the ordinary channel of communication with the United States government.
6.	A notice of motion has already been given calling for a return of certain documents and correspondence in connection with the appointment of the minister.
7.	No other appointments of ministers are under consideration at the present time.
8.	Answered under No. 7.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (Peace River) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the commencement forthwith and the completion in the near future of a direct railway outlet from the Peace river country to the Pacific coast.
He said:	It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to detain the House at any great length on the subject matter of this motion, because it has been before the House, though not in this particular form, for the last four or five years.
The Peace river country lies in the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, just east of the Rockies, and from four to seven hundred miles north of the international boundary. There is settled in that district approximately two million acres of land-two million acres of land as easily developed as any part of the prairie provinces, and with just as great possibilities as any other portion of like acreage anywhere within those provinces. It has been said that a great deal of this land is covered with bush. While there is a large part of the country covered with light brush, that is not true of the two million acres that is already settled. Approximately eighty per cent of this is simply covered with light bluffs and they are not in any sense a real detriment to the development of the country. That country is chiefly a farming country so far. We have, of course, the fishing industry. In Lesser Slave lake they have taken out as much as 1,200,000 pounds per annum. That quantity was reduced some years ago to one-half of that amount, because it was felt that 1,200,000 pounds annually was a little too heavy for the production of the lake. We have the lumbering industry, and there is a tremendous amount of timber. It has been estimated that in some districts not very far from Grande Prairie the amount of timber runs up into the billions of feet. It has been remarked by visitors who came into the country in 1910, when the rush of settlement started in that district, and by those who came in in later years after the war, that there was more permanent development in the Peace river country during that period than possibly in any other section of the prairie provinces in the same length of time. This is partly accounted for by the fact that there is timber in the country and it provides cheap material -to build homes. It is also accounted for by the fact that a country where the land is rich and where there is a reasonable number of trees tends to encourage people to develop homes, rather -than to make them merely speculators who prove up, then sell their lands and go elsewhere.
It has been said by a large number of people who have studied immigration and the settlement of the country that there are always three classes of settlers, first, the homesteader, then the man who buys from the homesteader and develops the land and lastly, the farmer.
Peace River Railway

So far as the Peace river country is concerned that is not so. After the war, of course, we had deflation. In the years 1922 and 1924 we had dry seasons. These two factors made for U3 possibly as difficult times as any part of the country ever had, and a large number-of people left the country, but in only very few cases did the original pioneers leave. They are practically all there stall. It is not surprising, possibly, in view of the fact that most of them went into the country over a trail three hundred miles long, which was jokingly referred to once by an Irishman as a " mud canal ". We think most of the settlers who would have proved inefficient as actual settlers did not get to the country at all. We have a population there to-day of approximately 20,000. The main industry, of course, is farming. We are located an average distance of about 1,600 miles from the head of the lakes. We are located geographically within 800 miles of the Pacific ports, but an order -to get to the Pacific ports we have to travel by railway a distance of 1,200 or 1,300 miles. There has been a rather intensive agitation for a direct connection with the Pacific coast during the last five years. That agitation has had some effect. We have received a great deal of support from the newspapers, and may I say that we have received very excellent support from the Southam press last year, Mr. Southam and some of his editors took a trip up through the Peace river country and gave us some veiy excellent publicity.
The country is served by the Edmonton, Dun vegan and British Columbia railway, which runs northwest for a distance of 300 or 400 miles into t'he Peace river country. Up until November 1926 the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia was operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway. In November 1926 it was taken over by the provincial government and is now operated by the provincial government through its Department of Railways and in close association or affiliation with the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National is the railway which can give us proper connection with the Pacific coast, because they can give us the direct connection that we ask for by the construction of approximately 168 miles up to 200 miles. I know that is the minimum mileage. But the country is well served to-day, or would be, with the construction of say another 400 miles of construction by branch railways. That is the settled portion of it, and if we had in addition to that a direct connection with the coast we would have a loop or semicircle formed by the road running northwest from Edmonton and that running southwest

to the British Columbia coast. I have said that this agitation has 'been carried on for four or five years and we have heard declarations made by public men in the west regarding this Peace river outlet. It has been the chief plank in the platform of both Liberal and Conservative candidates in the Peace river constituency in the last two elections. We have had statements regarding the Peace river railway from the Prime Minister in the city of Edmonton, as well as from Mr. Meighen when he was leader of the opposition. I have here the statement made by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King in Edmonton and reported in the Edmonton Bulletin on November 11th, 1924, and I quote the following:
King pledges self to the Peace river cause.
These are merely headings.
Premier promises outlet to Pacific;
Just as soon as humanly possible.
Railway will be built, declares Prime Minister, at mass meeting here.
Government has but minority in Commons; says times are now difficult and everybody must have a little patience, but Liberal party is not falling down on any of its pledges.
Here is the direct quotation:
"It is the policy of the government of which I have the honour to be the head to introduce a vigorous policy of immigration which will people the vast areas of undeveloped country in the great west," declared the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Premier of Canada, when addressing mass meeting of citizens in the First Presbyterian church last night.
What is the date?

October 11th, 1924, at
the First Presbyterian church in Edmonton. The quotation continues:
There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace river country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace river country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied and will open up the country for prospective settlers. I must, however, sound the same note to you here as I did to the citizens of Saskatoon. The times that we are passing through are very difficult, and I would ask you to have a little patience and in as short a time as possible a railway outlet will be provided for Peace river and northern Alberta districts that will open up an era of prosperity for that country which will not be equalled by any other province in Canada.
A "little patience" in 1924 and the railway would be built "as soon as humanly possible". That is a very sweeping statement and I think I am safe in saying thait the terms of my

Peace River Railway
motion are strictly within the terms of this pledge given by the right hon. Prime Minister at Edmonton in 1924.
Mr. Meighen made a trip west and he also said something regarding the Peace river outlet. This quotation is from Mr. Meighen's speech delivered at Edmonton October 1, 1925, and is taken from the literature of the Conservative candidate, in 1925, Mr. Collins:
X have always urged that the north country should have railway relief. I cannot be accused of making futile promises such as the Hon. Mackenzie King promised in the speech from the throne at the opening of the last session of parliament when he stated that he was going to give railway relief to the north country, and nothing has been done. This great question has been sidetracked by Senate reform, which subject has been discussed for forty years.
I may say that on the strength of that statement Mr. Collins, promised, not one outlet but two-one east of the mountains and one west. The Liberal candidate in 1926 -and I am sure the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) will recognize his picture- said this:
Pacific Coast Outlet: I consider this is the only solution for the financial difficulties of the people of the northern part of this riding, and I will do my utmost to get some definite action on it if elected. . . . For years the Peace river country has suffered the iniquity of oppressive freight rates and lack of transportation facilities. For years the northern people have valiantly tolerated these conditions and have fought with great tenacity for their removal. In a measure they have been successful, but much yet remains to be done. The coast connection alone stands between the Peace river people and wholesale prosperity.

What did you do
yourself?

(continuing reading):
At this election your vote will decide whether that measure of prosperity will accrue to you now or never in this generation. Weigh these bald facts, Mr. Voter. Do not lose sight of the fact that if we secure a coast connection it will be the Canadian National that will furnish it. Do not lose sight of the fact that Mackenzie King appointed Sir Henry Thornton, and that the Liberal government's courageous policy of national ownership has revealed a most astounding success.
What about myself, the hon. member asks. Neither in 1925 nor in 1926 did I promise more than I am doing at the present time. I stated that I was quite satisfied with the Right Hon. Mackenzie King's declaration of 1924, and would do my best to see that he lived up to it. That is my purpose in bringing forward this resolution.
It is fair, I think, to state that the federal government settled the Peace river country. A lot of people have asked why we were
foolish enough to go back three hundred miles from a railway. Well, at that time the lands were thrown open by the Dominion government, that is, in 1910, 1911 and 1912. Both Liberal and Conservative governments helped to settle that country. The ministers of the interior under those respective governments were the Hon. Frank Oliver and the Hon. Robert Rogers. There was a survey made of the Canadian Northern railway that ran northwest from Edmonton and right through Grande Prairie, across the mountains and out somewhere to the Pacific coast. I myself saw men in 1912 buying right-of-way in Grande Prairie, and they said three years was the limit we would have to wait for a railway.
So far as I am aware the entire expenditures of the federal government towards supplying that country with railway facilities is a grant of $5,000 a mile in connection with the line running from Spirit river down to Grande Prairie, a distance of some 50 or 60 miles, representing approximately $300,000. The provincial government has spent in the neighbourhood of $19,000,000 in providing railway facilities for that country. The federal government saddled the province with the responsibility, and I think it is up to the federal government to assume some further obligation with regard to the continued development of the Peace river district. The railways in the province of Alberta run northwest almost to the boundary of the province, and the only railway facilities the settlers have on the British Columbia side is the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway. The Alberta government cannot be expected to build railways through British Columbia. In addition to the grant of $300,000 that I have mentioned-that is not the exact sum, but it is approximately correct -the federal government voted $50,000 in 1923 for a survey of the various routes from the Peace river country to the Pacific coast, and in 1924 it voted an additional $75,000.
In 1925 we had tabled in this House the joint report of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific engineers who were sent out to make a survey of the country in order to ascertain what would be the most economical route to build and operate, particularly with the view of avoiding duplication. That joint report is somewhat canny and careful in its recommendations, but its authors go so far as to admit that the railway is justified. Unquestionably there is enough territory there to justify these transportation "facilities. There is a rich territory to be served, and it will be a revenue producer to the Canadian National Railway system. Indeed I do not know of
Peace River Railway

any better revenue producing territory for the Canadian National main line running from Edmonton to Prince Rupert than the Peace river country. In 1914 the first car of wheat was shipped from the north side of the Peace river. The wheat was grown in my own district. In 1921 about two and a half million bushels of grain were shipped out; in 1923 about three and a half million bushels; in 1926 it is estimated that about six million bushels have been hauled out. In addition to that the wheat is generally of very high quality. If there was ever any doubt at all about the possibilities of Peace River, it was surely dissipated last year, because Herman Trelle at Wembley near the present terminus of the Edinontonr-Dunvegan railway, captured the sweepstakes at Chicago m both wheat and oats, this being the first occasion on which one farmer has ever done that in the history of that grain show. This is the second time that Pence River has secured the sweepstakes in wheat, the first occasion being m 1883 when wheat from a district north of Peace Raver won .the first prize at a fair in Philadelphia.
There is an interesting report by Mr. Macoun, published in Ottawa on December 15, 1903, illustrating how pessimistic people can be sometimes regarding the future possibilities of a country. This gentleman was sent to make a survey of the Peace river district, and the impression he conveys in this article is shared, I think, :by many people throughout Canada even to-day. Many people still have the same feeling regarding the Peace river country. It is so far away, so near the north pole that there -must be something wrong with it. This report was not distributed. I believe it was suppressed by the minister of that day, and it was well that it was because it nas been shown to be entirely wrong. This is what he said:
While the country that has been described should, m the opinion of the writer, not be settled by either the rancher or the grower of wheat until there is more satisfactory evidence that it is suited for either of these pursuits, it may be safely prophesied that after railways have been built there will be only a very small part of it that will not afford homes for hardy northern people, who never having had much will be satisfied with little. It is emphatically a poor man's country, a country where any hard-working man may, in a few years, gather around him a few head of stock-horses, cattle and hogs-where he will be able to grow vegetables and in most years barley and oats and sometimes even wheat. But it will be many years before anything can be grown for export, even with good transport facilities. The building of the railway will lead to the development of the mines in northern British Columbia, and these mines will afford a market for beef and pork at least; but until there is some such mar-
ket, cash will be very scarce. During the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, there will of course be a ready market for any produce grown near the route it will follow, but such a market cannot last more than a year or two and the demand for food products will cease when the road is completed.
I have often thought of that statement when reading the engineers' report, and I will refer to it a little later. I have already said that we have 2,000,000 acres of settled land in the Peace river country, of which 150,000 acres are under cultivation. This year we have produced about 6,000,000 bushels of grain for export. The province of Alberta has about 29,000,000 acres settled, and in 1924 there were about ten or eleven million acres under cultivation, from which the province produced something like 131,000,000 bushels of gram, about half of that being wheat. I have said before that the 2,000,000 acres settled in the Peace river country can be developed just as easily as the 29,000,000 acres settled in Alberta, if not more easily, and with a reasonable and steady price for wheat, if the wheat pool lasts, you will see a wonderful development in that part of the Dominion.
The engineers' report goes on to state that we should wait until there is sufficient tonnage in the Peace river country to justify the railway. Well, there never would have been a railway built in Canada-at least, few would have been built-if we had always taken that attitude towards railway construction. Certainly the Canadian Pacific was not built under any such restriction, nor was the Grand Trunk Pacific nor the Canadian Northern. The fact is that settlement and railway development must proceed together if we are to have a healthy and reasonable development of the country. It has often been said that a large program of railway construction has led us into great difficulties. It was not the railway construction but the wrong location of the railways, and extravagance in connection with the building of them. I do not think there is a mile too much of railway in Canada to-day. The railways, are located in a great many instances in the wrong places.
There are three routes recommended by the engineers' report. One route is by Obed, running south from the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, east of the mountains. It would use the Edmonton-Dunvegan section of the railway running up through Grande Prairie and the Central Canada railway, which is a branch of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, as the branch line system for the present. That route is about 200 miles shorter to Pacific ports than the present route. The route that has been surveyed through Monk-

man pass, and which does not call for a larger expenditure than the completed Obed route, would bring the whole Peace river country within about 800 to 890 miles of the Pacific coast and is nearly 400 miles shorter than the present route. They are able to ship their grain out, even paying the excessive cost of transportation to the head of the lakes, and notwithstanding that cost they can make a small margin of profit. But if grain goes down to a dollar a bushel, even those who are located near the best transportation facilities will find it difficult indeed to send their grain out and secure any return. So that the comparison which the minister makes, based upon the report, and which I am really surprised that engineers of such standing should submit in regard to the saving between the increased interest charges on capital investment and the calculation based upon the present volume of traffic, is wholly false. The only reason in the world

Peace River Railway
why we would ask for the completion of the road lies in the hope of'having an increased traffic. No one in his senses would suggest building the road in there at a cost of thirteen million dollars to serve the present volume of traffic, for that is an absurd position to take. I say it is absurd for these engineers to take that position.
They do not.
That is the way the minister presented the matter.

No. The words used
by the engineers are "assumed initial traffic." If my hon. friend will permit me I will give him the engineers' words; I will tell him what the engineers take as their basis for the term "assumed initial traffic."

It is exactly what I am
saying-the assumed initial traffic. I will take my hon. friend's own words.
If the hon. member will let me inform him he will not fall into error.

My hon. friend would
not allow me to interrupt him, or even to ask him a question.

If I owe the hon. member an apology I offer it now. I know, however, that he wants his statement to be fair to the engineers. The engineers say:
We have therefore for our studies assumed an initial outgoing traffic to the Pacific seaboard about five times as large as that indicated in the previous table, showing shipments during five years ending with the crop of 1923.
That is to say, in dealing with the assumed initial traffic they are taking a tonnage five times larger than the average of the five years ending in 1923. I merely want my hon. friend to have correct information.

The minister says that
the assumed initial traffic is based upon a tonnage five times greater than the average of the five years up to 1923.
That is what the report says.

Well, that is what the minister bases his argument upon. Now, if I am not greatly mistaken-I have not had time to look into the question-more wheat went out in 1926 than in the preceding years. In 1926, six million bushels were shipped out whereas the amount that went out in the previous years was very much less.
That is true.

I still submit that the
basis of the minister's argument is absurd. Notwithstanding all the handicaps of the last ten or fifteen years-not of the last two years, because they have been less serious in that time-20,000 settlers have stuck to their guns. They have tried to make things go, to increase production, and tens of thousands more are ready to go into that country if it is given such transportation facilities as nature affords it. That is the point I make, and to base the whole argument of a report, which is supposed to be accurate, upon an assumption of a tonnage five times greater than the average of five years that were very much leaner than the present, is absurd.
It appeals to me that the proposition narrows itself down to this: you have a magnificent country ready for settlement, a country that is well developed, and known to the world, known I think all over the globe as the choicest section of the North American continent, where good land can be had cheaply from one of the last remaining large areas. And in that section there is already a settlement of 20,000 people. All that is required to make that area accessible to the markets of the world is the construction of a few hundred miles of railway at a cost of $13,000,000. That construction would accomplish two things: it would give to these 20,000 settlers, who went there on guarantees of the service, something to which they are entitled, namely, access to the markets of the world. And ,in the second place, it would do something greater for Canada, for it would open up a virgin territory which is exceedingly attractive and which offers opportunities for great returns.
Now I urge the minister and the government to give this matter their consideration. I am not going to compare this section with others, nor am I going to draw any comparison between this suggested work and work which is authorized, or which may be authorized, elsewhere. I do say, however, that I know of no area in Canada to-day that offers greater possibilities than, the Peace river country. I know of no territory that would be more readily settled by immigrants than that country, if this question were solved. I know of no territory of similar extent that can be so cheaply brought into active productivity.
I want to give one or two figures. The minister suggested to the committee that with present rates the farmers could move their products to the markets of the world as cheaply as if they had connection with the Pacific coast. This, surely, cannot be sound.

Peace River Railway
The mileage from Grande Prairie, the centre of the district, to Fort William is 1,600 miles, while the mileage to the Pacific coast, if this new connection were made, would be 800 miles, or one-half the distance. The maximum grade to the Pacific coast is one-half of one per cent, according to this report of the engineers. In other words it is really a water grade to the Pacific, being practically level. On the other hand, there are adverse grades on the prairies, going to Fort William, which are much higher. So that the question of grade does not enter into the discussion at all. The grade is Al; nothing better could be wished for; and the distance is one-half that to Fort William. Now, if you are going to haul grain 1,600 miles to Fort William-I do not care what rate you get-when you could haul it 800 miles to the other point, some one is going to pay the difference in cost between these mileages. The cost will be made up from some source. In other words, assuming that the inference drawn by the minister is correct-and, by the way, I dispute it-if these people can send their grain to Fort William as cheaply as they can to the Pacific coast, then they are getting a rate far below that given anyone else on the prairies.

My hon. friend is misquoting me entirely. I never discussed the question of shipping grain to Fort William but to the Pacific coast via Edmonton. I made no comparisons based on shipments to Fort William.

To the Pacific coast via Edmonton, then. The mileage to the Pacific coast via Edmonton is 1,200 and the minister says that they will haul grain from the Peace river country 1,200 miles as cheaply as they would be able to get it out if this connection were miade giving a haul of 800 miles.
I did not say that either.

I am narrowing the
minister down to this fact, which he should have stated, that there would be a distinct saving to these settlers if they had this cutoff. The minister sought to leave the impression with the House that there would be no saving; I leave it to the House if that is not so. He did not say it in so many words, but when I rose to put the straight question he would not let me speak, saying that he was making an intricate argument and did not wish to be interrupted. I say now that there would be a distinct saving to the settlers of the Peace river country if this connection were made, and there would also be such an 
impetus given immigration that it would mark an epoch in this country.
Now I am going to make a suggestion to the House and to the mover of this resolution, which I urge the minister to receive kindly. I make this suggestion on my own responsibility; I have not consulted my leader, whom perhaps I should have asked, but nevertheless this is my view. It is a simple suggestion, which I hope will be found acceptable. We have a committee of this House which is appointed year by year to deal with the problems of the Canadian National railways; to this committee are usually referred the railway estimates and other similar matters. I consider this matter to be of such great importance and to affect the lives of thousands of people so seriously, as well as to offer such magnificent opportunities, that it should be directly referred to this committee with instructions to inquire carefully into it and ito examine the reports Which have been presented, as well as the engineers themselves if necessary. Then the committee could bring into this House some recommendation dealing with the question. I think this is a reasonable suggestion, -and one which should be accepted. A moment ago the minister stated that if this came to a vote he would have to vote 'against it, and of course in saying that he asked all his supporters to do the same.
No.

I do not want to see the House reject this motion; I would not like to see it voted down, because in a sense it would be a repudiation of a suggestion which I think merits more consideration than that. By sending this matter to a committee, which I .think should be called together very soon, an opportunity would be given those interested to present their case, and at least that degree of consideration would be given.
Mr. JAMES C. BRADY (Skeena): Before I deal with the subject under discussion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to dissociate from it the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). I believe he has given us not his own opinion but what information he has obtained from a report made to him.
Having done this, I would like to enumerate the various reasons advanced from the report, why the development of the Peace river district should not be commenced immediately.
I think these reasons were very well emphasized, and are thoroughly understood even by those not directly interested. It was said that the president and engineers of the Canadian National Railways did not deem it an economic possibility; that it would not lower

Peace River Railway
the present rates; that it would cost about $13,000,000, and that the present volume of traffic does not -permit the development of this district. I would like to -ask the House if any one of these reasons has sufficient weight to prevent this necessary development of the greatest agricultural area in Canada. Without going into figures, M-r. Speaker, I think I could give four or five reasons which would make the government consider the necessity of immediately dealing with this question,.
The Peace River development is not a local matter; it has a national importance, because it would almost double the present area under grain in Canada. Then it would also assist the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) in overcoming the many handicaps in the way of an up to date immigration scheme, which is practically essential. This development is necessary to the interests of the Canadian National Railways, as well, -because, it would add to the present volume of trade running -over this road to the Pacific coast, and is a sufficient warranty for this work. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) said something with which I quite agree and which I think everyone appreciated, when he asked, "Should we start with immigration first, put the people on the land and wait till they make good, or should we at the same time give those people opportunities to develop their land more quickly an-d -bring returns to the railways?"
I do not intend to speak further on this matter, Mr. Speaker, -but there is one other reason which I think the government should consider -carefully. In Prince Rupert we have an elevator which in the last four months has handled a little over 2,750,000 bushels of grain from Alberta; now that the elevator is there it must stay -there, and it is the duty of the government to see that this elevator is able to continue to function.
It is the imperative task and duty of the government to develop the western part of the Peace river district which, by every proof that can be and has been advanced, has been shown to be the most productive agricultural area in Canada. I have therefore great pleasure in supporting the resolution of the hon. member for Peace River, and I do so, not merely on behalf of the incoming immigrants, not merely because of an extra six .million bushels of wheat that may come, but on behalf of the development of Canada and the natural resources which are there ready for the settler if he be given but a chance. In the development of the Peace river country
we have an opportunity of great moment. If we make an investment of $13,000,000, in a few years we shall be rewarded beyond our most sanguine expectations. This is not a party question but it is a question that strikes deep at the root of the future development, growth and prosperity of Canada as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I am very much disappointed at the report that these eminent engineers have given in relation to the railway problem of developing the Peace river country. I also notice that very little attention has been paid to a certain project that we have in British Columbia, namely, the Pacific Great Eastern railway. Mention has been made of the Edmonton and Dunvegan railway, but very little has been said of the Pacific 'Great Eastern railway. Let me remind the House that when these two railways were undertaken, the Pacific Great Eastern by the province of British Columbia and the Edmonton and Dunvegan by the province of Alberta, they were to connect at the boundary between these two provinces, forming a continuous line of transportation from the Peace river country to the Pacific as well as from the Peace river country to Edmonton. Both of these projects unfortunately have fallen short of their destination and they both remain at the present time up in the air.
I might say a word or two in regard to the early history of that part of the country. The province of British Columbia was opened up in the first place by way of the Peace river pass, the very pass to which all these railroads are pointing at the present time. The elevation of the Peace river pass is 2,500 feet, not a very great elevation, in fact the lowest point there is in the Rocky mountains on the North American continent. It seems to me surprising that these eminent engineers, with only that elevation to overcome, have not directed the attention of the people of Canada to the Peace river pass. The Peace river passes through the Rocky mountains at Hudson Hope. That is the eastern breaking of the Peace river canyon. You go up the Peace river and then you follow up the Parsnip river until you come to Summit lake. From that point you have only seven miles of a portage in order to reach the Fraser river. The elevation at that point is 2,500 feet. With all deference to the eminent engineers I believe the Peace river country should properly be opened up by the easiest natural route, which is the Peace river and the Fraser river, the following of each of those water courses from the coast to the Peace river country
Peace River Railway

The Peace river country is an immense country, probably 400 miles long on each side [DOT] of the river by 100 miles in width, and it is capable of vast development. Indeed, as has been pointed out here to-day, it is easily conceivable that it might double the production of grain in the Dominion of Canada. That being so, surely the idea of spending $13,000,000 is not going to stop the development of a country of that kind. What is the matter with the people of the Dominion of Canada? What is the matter with this government of the Dominion? Is that the spirit in which the Canadian Pacific undertook to open up the prairies of the west. We have a question of spending only $13,000,000 to complete this project and still the government says: Oh, it is too much.
On the other hand what do we find? The other day we were asked to vote $12,000,000 for the port of Montreal and in another case we were asked to vote $14,000,000 for work on the Welland canal. It is conceded as a matter of fact that the opening of the Welland canal is not going to cheapen the transportation of grain to the port of Montreal by a fraction of a cent per bushel. Still we are spending $15,000,000 a year and we have already spent some $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 on it. But when we have a question of opening up an outlet for this great empire in the western part of the country we cannot do anything with it. With all deference to everyone's opinion I believe there is no question that the Peace river development not only in Alberta, but also the development that will follow in British Columbia, will more than warrant any expenditure that is necessary to complete a project of that kind.
The Peace river development is not a very new matter so far as I am concerned.. In the year 1891 I went to the town of Quesnel which is on the Fraser river some ninety miles south of Prince George. I went into commercial business in that town, and in the course of my business there at that date, before the completion of the Calgary and Edmonton railway, I sold goods, I loaded goods on scows in the town of Quesnel and had them transported into the Peace river country in order to provide that country with necessaries of life. They would go in in the fall and come out again the following spring with furs in return for the goods which they had brought in. Does that not point to the fact that the Fraser river and Peace rivet route affords a natural access to the Peace river country?
I might say a good deal more in connection with this matter, but the principal thing I

have to say is to express my disappointment not only with the action ;of the government, but also with the report of the engineers. My own personal opinion is that that report is not of very much value, and that the subject has not been studied from as many angles as possible. For instance, I understood from the Minister of Railways that the Pine river pass route had been thrown to one side entirely, discarded as impossible and impracticable. If I am not fight, the minister will correct me.
That is scarcely a correct quotation from the engineers' report. They discarded that route because of the manifest advantages, comparatively speaking, of the Monkman pass route.

It is the Pine pass route
I am speaking of.

That was not discarded
because it was quite impracticable. According to the engineers, the Monkman route is so much superior, and so nearby, that it was not necessary to go into detail in the report on the Pine pass route.

The minister was speaking
of the Monkman pass route, and be gave us no estimate of the Pine pass route at all. Might I ask if there is an estimate of the cost of that route in the report?

I shall be very glad to
read What the report says in regard to the matter. It says:
The only advantage which the Pine pass route has over the Peace pass route is that it would be shorter for traffic originating south of the Peace river. There is no feasible crossing of the Peace river between Peace river crossing and the Canyon at Hudson Hope.
That is correct.

It continues:
-and on account of the high country between the latter point and the Pine pass, the line would have to return east for a considerable distance on the south side of the river before the ground becomes low enough between it and the Pine river to allow of a feasible line south to the Pine river valley. The recently discovered Monkman pass is in turn more advantageous than the Pine pass for this traffic on account of its lesser gradients and distance. Pine pass is approximately 175 miles from, and nearly due west of Spirit river, and approximately 155 miles nearly due north of Prince George.
They do not give any estimated costs of the Pine pass route, for the reasons there stated, but the Peace pass is fully dealt with and I can give my hon. friend the figures if he desires them.

Peace River Railway

They considered that it
would 'be a great deal more expensive than the Monkman pass route.

Yes, $21,000,000 for the
initial development as against $13,000,000.

Noth withstanding the comparatively larger cost, when you consider this question from the point of view of the province of British Columbia, and British Columbia must be taken into consideration as well, because you come very close to a section of British Columbia which is very highly mineralized-let me interject just here the prophecy that if the proper railway development is given to that part of the country you may see in the Omineca district another development such as we have in Trail today; that is quite within the realms of possibility; indeed, it is very probable-I say that that section of the country Should be connected up with the Pacific coast. I know perfectly well from travelling through the Peace river country both in Alberta and British Columbia that that is the objective of every person in the Peace river country. They say that they went in there with the promise of a railway outlet in a very short time.
Which route do the majority of the settlers now in the Peace river country favour?

So far as the settlers in
any part of the Peace river country are concerned, they favour no particular route. What they want is connection with the Pacific coast, and they leave to the proper authorities the selection of the most feasible route..
Again, take the railway which was started by the province of British Columbia, the Pacific and Great Eastern. Some people call it British Columbia's white elephant; in fact, that is what our own government out there calls it, but let me tell the people here that so far as I am concerned the Pacific and Great Eastern is no white elephant at all. What is troubling British Columbia at the present time is the white elephant of a government that we have there, and if we could only get rid of our white elephant government we might have reasonable railway development.
I have had much pleasure in listening to the debate on this question this afternoon. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is a very good one. I know perfectly well that so far as I am concerned this is a question that has not been examined as thoroughly as it should have been, and it has not .received the consideration to which it is entitled, nor have the people of the Peace river country received the consideration to which they are entitled. I therefore think that the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is a very reasonable one, that this question should be referred to the special railway committee. In conclusion, I must say that I have very much pleasure in supporting the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) in any effort he may make for the opening up of that territory by means of a railway outlet, which has been promised so many times.

In rising to say a few words on this resolution, I may say at the outset that if the matter comes to a vote, I am prepared to support the resolution as it stands. Failing that I will support the proposal made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens).
I am prepared to support the resolution as it stands because the report of the engineers from which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has quoted shows conclusively that a line of railway can be built through this territory by one or more alternative routes and at a moderate cost. Take, for instance, the Sturgeon lake and Obed route, which the minister states is approximately 200 miles, and the cost of which is approximately $13 000,000. That line can therefore be built at a cost of approximately $65,000 per mile or $35,000 per mile less than the country paid for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific-approximately the same amount as the Canadian Northern paid for the construction of their line of railway through the province of British Columbia.
I support the resolution secondly for the reason that a railway outlet would, in the words of the Prime Minister, open up for development an empire. I note that the hon. member for Peace River, speaking before an audience in Edmonton, stated that the Prime Minister said:
The Peace river is among the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity.
I am in entire agreement with the statement of the Prime Minister, and for these two reasons I am prepared to support the motion of the hon. member for Peace River that this railway be built now.
It may be asked, how can you favour this course in view of the engineers' report and in view of the statements made by the. hon. Minister of Railways. Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying
Peace River Railway

that this report from which the Minister of Railways has quoted is absolutely misleading. Rather I would put it this way: that this report is of no value from a commercial point of view. Perhaps the Minister of Railways will correct me if I am wrong in the deductions I make from the report. I observe that the report states that the average tonnage available for la period of five years, ending 1923-
What page?

I am quoting from the typewritten copy, page 13. It may correspond with the report the minister has. It states that the average tonnage available is 48,934 tons, or a total of 2,043,000 bushels of grain. Now then, the minister stated that the engineers had allowed five times that amount as the initial traffic which would be available. I notice that they place the tonnage at 35,000 tons-that is at page 25-and they multiply that by five, making a total of 175,000 tons available. On page 13 the report States that the average tonnage over the period of five years up to 1923 was 48,934, or 13,934 tons greater than that allowed by the engineers. As a matter of fact, on the figures quoted by the member for Peace river, the number of bushels taken out of the Peace river in the year 1926 amounted to 6,000,000, or three times the tonnage that was available on the average of the five years quoted. That would make a tonnage of grain alone for the year 1926 of 146,000, which is almost equal to the amount which the engineers report to this House as being five times that presently available. In other words, the tonnage for this year of grain alone almost equals that which these engineers state to be five times the amount presently available.
My hon. friend must bear in mind that this report was made in February of 1925.
I appreciate that; I am giving the year and trying to show that there, has been that development since.
That is the point.
Which shows that the report is of little practical value to us.
They should make it five times that this year.

Exactly what I am coming to. There is another respect in which this report fails-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong, because I have not had an opportunity of making a careful analysis and study of it.
 .
My hon. friend was not wrong.

I am right so far, and I have the concurrence of the minister. My next point is that I think it a well-recognized principle that there would be available approximately three hundred per cent more tonnage on all commodities carried than would be carried in grain alone.
Three hundred per cent?

Yes, three times. In other words, if the railway carried a tonnage of grain of 150,000 tons, which they would carry this year, they would carry of all commodities in and out approximately 450,000 tons. I think my hon. friend from Peace River will have figures to show that that was approximately the percentage of increase carried by the railway company in all commodities.
If I am right in that respect, I want to carry my argument one step further. The figures supplied by the railway engineers allow that country a production of approximately two million bushels of grain. This year, two years after the report wias made, we find an increase of three hundred per cent, despite the tremendous disadvantage that country is suffering from-three hundred per cent in two years' time. I think the House will agree with me-and in fact I think it is admitted by the Prime Minister and in all the reports- that Peace River is one of the richest grain countries in the world, and if there are over two million acres presently available for cultivation if properly tapped by the railways, that the production of wheat and other grain in that district would be not less than fifty million bushels, or twenty-five times the average tonnage estimated by these engineers two years ago in grain alone. In addition of course this government must take hold of the situation and undertake a colonization scheme, because conditions in that country warrant a colonization scheme if it is warranted in any part of Canada. I ask this government, where to-day in Canada are there lands that equal in quality the lands in the Peace river district available for colonization? Where to-day are there lands that are available at as cheap a price as the lands in that district? Where to-day has the Dominion government an area of land under its own jurisdiction which can be used for immigrants? Where else can such land be found? I think, Mr. Speaker, we can safely state that there is no other part of Canada that presents such a fertile field for immigration as does the Peace river country, and it is dependent entirely, as the Prime Minister himself said in addressing

Peace River Railway
an audience in Edmonton, on an outlet to the Pacific coast, which he stated at that time was an absolute necessity.
We have this afternoon emphasized the resources of that country for grain alone, but we all know that it has immense mineral wealth and immense timber wealth, either of which might justify the building of a railway. These two subjects have not been touched upon, but they are resources which would provide a tremendous increase in the tonnage. Without, however, allowing a single ton for minerals and timber, we will find that colonized for agricultural purposes alone the country will provide a tonnage twenty-five to thirty times greater than that upon which the engineers based their estimate. That being the case there should be, when that country is colonized, a tonnage in agricultural products alone and those necessarily handled m conjunction therewith, in excess of thirteen million. In this report the engineers admit that when the tonnage equals 1,400,000 tons it will be economically unsound to haul via Edmonton over the Edmonton and Dunvegan route.
Now, it is very clear that if this country is colonized and developed to anything like its capacity there will be, based on agriculture alone, a total tonnage in the not far distant future, ten times greater than that referred to by the engineers as being sufficient to justify the building of this outlet. Just visualize, Mr. Speaker, what that railway would mean not only to the people who are there to-day, but to the development of Canada generally and to the Canadian National Railway. It is well known that no railway in this country has prospered which did not have feeders or branch lines. On the Canadian National Railway we have one stretch in excess of 700 miles which has no feeder or branch line. We come here now asking for a branch line leading into one of the richest parts of the Dominion, and the minister stands in his place and calmly says that for three years at least, based upon this report, we should not consider the building of this railway.

Mr. Speaker, again my
hon. friend is misquoting me. I read Sir Henry Thornton's opinion that the existing arrangement with the Alberta government operating its own railway might very well work for the next three years. I did not express an opinion of that kind myself.

I thought the minister was
really basing his conclusions upon this report. I have not the letter of Sir Henry Thornton before me, but I feel convinced he must be basing his opinion upon this report.
That is right.

Then that is good enough. It is perfectly clear, I think, to anyone who has made even a cursory study of the report that it is' not worth the paper it is written on for the purpose of arriving at a sound conclusion as to whether or not this railway should be built. There is information in it of inestimable value, but from the point of view of whether the railway would be an economically sound project or not I feel the report is of no great value to this House.
There are several other aspects of this report that I might touch upon, but I have dealt with what I consider the fundamental feature of it. If there is any portion of Canada where additional railway construction is justified and requires immediate investigation it is in this particular part of the country. I repeat, the Prime Minister considered that to be the case three years ago when he pledged himself that as soon as it was humanly possible the great Peace river country would be given that measure of railway relief that would bring to the pioneers of that country an outlet'that they had been so long denied and would open up the country for prospective settlers. What stronger pronouncement could we have? Am I to infer that the Minister of Railways disagrees with the policy announced by the Prime Minister on that occasion? It would appear so. It might be very interesting indeed to have a vote upon this resolution to see who on that side of the House are following the Prime Minister and who are following the Minister of Railways, because I do not think there could be any declarations of policy so diametrically opposed to each other than that announced by the Prime Minister at Edmonton and that which we have heard this afternoon from the Minister of Railways.
I urge upon this House, Mr. Speaker, the immediate and favourable consideration of this resolution. Failing that, I urge an immediate investigation before a committee as suggested by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens).

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess that
before hon. gentlemen had spoken I did not think there was any need for a further investigation, but the more statements I hear about the Peace river country and the proposed railways there the more I am in favour of the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) because I think there is a great deal of misinformation abroad in this House in relation to the subject.
Peace River Railway

Let me say at once that I am extremely interested in an outlet to the coast from the Peace river country. On various occasions I have pressed this matter upon the attention of my colleagues, and1 I do not believe the Peace river country will ever come into its own until there is such an outlet. But the suggestion of building the outlet by Obed or a connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway east of the Rocky mountains is not the solution of the question. Anyone who knows the country will say so immediately. So what is the use of discussing a $13,000,000 project which gets us nowhere? That is Why I say we need more information. As for the Monkman pass, practically the same thing can be said. It touches only the southwest comer of the Grande Prairie district, and would entail expensive railway building from the north side of the river, which is a huge agricultural territory that still needs railway construction. Going westward, it is admitted by everyone that you cannot cross the Peace river until you get in the vicinity of Hudson Hope. Therefore you are figuring not on 119 miles but on 150 miles more. I agree with the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) that the only feasible route, irrespective of what it costs, is by the Peace river pass. No one can deny that who knows the topography of the country and the direction in which the rivers run.
Surely the Alberta government has had experience enough in crossing the Peace river. When the estimate for the construction of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway was before the Alberta legislature it stood at $7,000,000. Well, hon. gentlemen from that province know that up to date it has cost almost three times what the engineers estimated at the outset. I am not interested in any engineers' figures because they are no guarantee of what the ultimate cost may be. I am not familiar with British Columbia, but I have been greatly impressed by the reports of what may be accomplished by going ahead and opening up the coal mining area in the Portland canal district and the mining territory between the head of the Parsnip river and the Portland canal in a direct route from the coast to the Peace river country.
May I say that the building of the line merely from the boundary of British Columbia to the coast is not the solution of the problem? A great deal has been said about the possibility of putting new settlers in that country if you complete that piece of construction. If the logical route is chosen you would have to connect the two lines at Hudson Hope and build one hundred miles north of the Peace river. There is no very desirable territory 
to be opened up over that whole hundred miles, but there is territory in British Columbia favourable for settlement that the line would render accessible. That is, in addition to building the line from the boundary of British Columbia to the coast, no matter what route you choose-and I am all for the Peace river -you would have to build additional lines into Alberta before you could put new settlers on crown lands. So I say all these things need investigation. If you were to build a line from Peace river crossing tfl Fort Vermilion you would open up an immense territory of some 300 miles of virgin land1 which could be devoted to cultivation. But it requires a railway to open up that land. After the experience we have had with the Peace river country, however, I am not one of those to encourage new settlers to take up homesteads in such territories in the hope of having railways built to them. There should be some more definite assurance than the settlers got in the Peace river country before people are induced to take a chance and wait years for railway development to enable them to ship their produce. We know that grain can be grown in the Peace river district. The Lawrences have been established for years and have been growing and milling grain, selling it to newcomers, in a district 300 miles north of Peace river. But these territories would all have to be opened up by rail.
I welcome the suggestion that a thorough investigation of the whole matter should be made before we plunge into an expenditure of thirty or forty million dollars, for it would mean that much; although, let me add, the district is worth that expenditure. When the railway is built there will be a period of years during which it will be neither more nor less than a colonization line, and will not pay interest on the bonded indebtedness. My hon. friend has pointed to the two existing railways. The Edmonton-Dunvegan, I would remind the House, is a heavy burden on the people of Alberta who have to carry the bonded indebtedness of this line, because it has done little so far besides paying operating and maintenance expenses. The Canadian Pacific, when the new lease was suggested, offered fifty or sixty thousand dollars towards the carrying charges of the bonded indebtedness, and inasmuch as they operated the line for five years they should have been in a favourable position to estimate what the road would be worth. The line to Obed, in my opinion, will be no solution, for the reason that it simply taps one corner of the Grande Prairie countiy and lines would have to be built across the Peace river to connect the north country with it. More than that, it

Peace River Railway
would result in a cut-up that would absolutely kill the usefulness of 300 miles of the Ed-monton-Dunvegan railway, and that is not to be desired by the people of Alberta.
I think a great deal more information is required if We are to come to a wise decision on this question. I am not one of those who are prepared to stand up and say that it will cost a small sum to open up the Peace river country. I do not think it will be inexpensive. I believe that at the earliest possible moment at which there is reasonable hope of providing an outlet the road should be built, but I am not ready to suggest that it should be this year. In fairness to the House we ought to recognize that the question involves far more than the mere construction of a line from the Peace river country to the coast. It is true we have an elevator at Prince Rupert, and I am pleased to learn that such a large volume of grain has passed through it. It has warranted its construction and the whole northern portion of Alberta is now producing well and will increase in production in the future by leaps and bounds, so that all these elevators on the coast will have been justified. I would point out to my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), that during the past two or three years little or no grain has passed through any portion of northern Alberta to Fort William. It is practically all routed to the coast, and will continue to be so shipped unless an embargo is put on to prevent the shipment of grain through the elevator at Prince Rupert.
No matter how much relief we are able to give the settlers in Peace river in the transportation of their grain by way of Edmonton they will always be under a handicap until an outlet is provided, for it is not possible to obviate that 400 miles of haulage, and the settlers will always suffer disabilities in that respect. I say, therefore, that if we are to undertake this project we should do so with our eyes open, fully realizing what it will cost. Even if it takes $40,000,000, the expenditure ultimately will be warranted, but it is idle to suggest that $30,000,000 will suffice. That is entirely out of the question. And further, if we are to place any considerable number of settlers on the land there it will mean additions to already existing branch lines.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Health and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on this
very important resolution, and first I would like to commend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) for having brought it before the House. He seemed to base his remarks on statements made at public meetings by the right hon. Prime Minister and the late Prime Minister, Mr. Meighen, when they suggested that the construction of a railway into the Peace river country, giving an outlet to the Pacific coast, should be undertaken forthwith. I do not think we should take exception to the remarks of either of these gentlemen, because we know they were aware of the importance of this matter not only to the people of the Peace river district but to those in Alberta, and British Columbia, and its indirect importance tQ the people of Canada as a whole. Believing that, I think they were well within their province when they stated that as leaders of great parties they were prepared to do what was in their power to bring about the early construction of this railway.
I think we must also take into consideration the statement made by my colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning); he was able in his address to lay before the House information secured from what might be considered the best channels available. In other words, at the conference already mentioned there were present the executives of the different railway companies, under the chairmanship of the then Minister of Railways, Right Hon. George P. Graham. In addition to Mr. Graham there were present Hon. Charles Stewart, Hon. J. H. King, Hon. John Oliver, Premier of British Columbia; Hon. H. Greenfield, Premier of Alberta; Hon. V. W. Smith, Minister of Railways and Telephones for Alberta; Sir Henry Thornton, President of the Canadian National Railways; S. J. Hungerford, Vice-President of the Canadian National Railways; C. J. Smith, executive assistant to the president of the Canadian National Railways; G. A. Bell, Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals; E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; Grant Hall, Vice President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; D. M. Kennedy, M.P. and W. F. Maclean, M.P. The meeting was held at 2.30 o'clock on January 9, 1925, and was called at the instigation of the government then in power. It was the desire of the government at that time to try, through the medium of these railway executives, to devise a plan whereby this great section of hinterland could be served by proper railway construction, it being the hope of the government that these men, with their vast experience, could bring forth some
Peace River Railway

such plan. So far as railway construction in Canada is concerned we have arrived at the stage to-day where the executives of the two great railways must take their responsibilities in advising the government on questions of importance.
At that conference it was decided that the presidents of the railways mentioned would place their engineering staffs on a basis of mutual co-operation to solve this problem. The Minister of Railways gave the House this afternoon, briefly but concisely, the information obtained in this way, which would indicate that it is not an expenditure of $13,000,000 or $20,000,000 which will solve this problem. An expenditure of $13,000,000 would give access by one route to the main line of the Canadian National railways, what is known as the old Grand Trunk Pacific, while an expenditure of $20,000,000 would give connection down through the Peace river pass to the Canadian National railways leading to Prince Rupert and Vancouver. But as I see the situation, Mr. Speaker, that merely gives an outlet to the territory which is at present adjacent to the lines of a railway already constructed, and does not deal with the larger question of a development of the Peace river country. Instead of an expenditure of $13,000,000 or $20,000,000 I am informed by that report that to develop that great country will require an expenditure of probably $50,000,000 or $60,000,000, if the lines suggested this afternoon were followed out. Such an expenditure should not give anyone any concern if it is shown that the construction will lead to the development of that great country, because we are informed that the area there is capable of a development which will pay veiy handsomely for such an expenditure.
In the few moments I have at my disposal I would also like to call to the attention of the House the efforts which have been made by the people of British Columbia and Alberta, through their governments, to solve this question. We find that there has been an expenditure of some $50,000,000 by those two provincial governments representing the people of those provinces. I wish to make this suggestion to the parliament of Canada and to the railway executives of this country, that in the solution of this question, that is, of providing proper transportation facilities to that country, the efforts and the expenditures that have been made by those provincial governments with the object of bringing about what we are to-day considering, should not be lost sight of, and that if it is possible to conserve those investments to the advantage

of the Canadian National Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway, whichever may undertake to develop that country, such conservation should be made.
I do not think the parliament of Canada should lightly brush aside expenditures made by those provinces in connection with the object which we are now considering. There is undoubtedly a great country to be served, a country which when opened up can be served advantageously by connection with the Pacific coast ports, and the people who are so fortunate as to go into that country and receive that service will, I believe, be probably better placed than some of those who may live and reside to-day in central Canada. I know there is a tendency in other portions of the northwest and of the prairie provinces to confine our settlement operations to areas already served by rail transportation; that as, that there may be a more concentrated centering of the population in those provinces. But I am satisfied that within the very near future, with conditions improving as they are in Canada, there will be a demand, and a proper demand, made for the earliest development of this great portion of Canada known as the Peace river country.
It is not for me to discuss the pass or channel which should be chosen in order that the outlet may be had. I was pleased to hear my colleague the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) this afternoon confirm the suggestion made by the hon. member for Caa-iboo (Mr. Fraser) that in his opinion-which dhould be worth. something to members of thus House because he has had large experience in the province of Alberta; probably no member has a larger knowledge than he has of that great country in the north-the Peace River pass, even though it may cost $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 more than the pass first mentioned, is undoubtedly one that should be considered in the development of that district. He also threw out the suggestion that it might be eventually found advisable to extend the line, not to the south, but directly west to the Portland canal or what is known as the Stewart terminus. That is a matter that should certainly receive our consideration and be thoroughly canvassed before parliament makes up its mind as to what developments should take place in that country. With the consent of my confrere the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), I am .going to suggest that we follow the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and rather than place this resolution to the view of the House at the present time, refer the matter to the committee on railways. Was that the one?

Peace River Railway

The suggestion was the
special committee. I would prefer the standing committee on railways and canals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The minister says he would prefer the standing committee on railways and oanals. That would meet with my approval, and I hope the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) will see the wisdom of that suggestion, because it will enable hon. members to secure further information on the subject; and it will be possible for them to call before the committee the various railway authorities and enable us to develop to a greater degree the knowledge that we have in regard to this important question.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the discussion upon this important question has proceeded in this chamber to-day, it is evident that the government is now inclined to appreciate the seriousness of the subject far more than it was at the outset of the debate. I remember that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) concluded his remarks this afternoon by stating that if this matter were pressed to a division he would be compelled reluctantly to vote against it. I a,m glad to congratulate the government that they have now had! new light upon the subject. The speeches this afternoon of members of this House coming from the district more particularly affected by th:s motion have been to my mind most convincing. I confess that I am not as familiar with the geography of the Peace river district as some hon. members are, but at the same time I have a fair idea of it. After hearing the statements as presented in this chamber this afternoon I am convinced that we have before us a very important question which should be settled in the near future.
The Minister of Health (Mr. King) commenced1 his remarks by saying that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) must have received some inspiration from speeches made in regard to this proposed development by the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) and from speeches made by the former Prime Minister of Canada during the election contest. I gathered that both of those right hon. gentlemen in those pre-election utterances committed themselves in regard to these various projects. The Minister of Health seems to draw a sharp distinction between a commitment made by the Prime Minister of this country in an election proceeding and a commitment made at any other 'time. A commitment made by a Prime Minister in the course of an election is of the most sacred 32649-18
character. If the present Prime Minister promised during the last or the preceding election to go ahead with the construction of this railway, the government is morally bound to proceed with it, and this House will not accept an explanation by the Minister of Railways, or the Minister of the Interior, or the Minister of Health, because they cannot explain away what was a clear commitment on the part of the head of the government of this country Had the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen been returned to power the promise would have been made good.
Oh, oh.

But when we speak of a promise mlade by a Prime Minister on the other side of the House, his colleagues laugh; they treat it as a joke. One of the most serious criticisms that can be levelled against this government for the last six years is that they have always been inclined to treat their promises somewhat lightly, and this is just another evidence of their weakness in that respect- This report, I am told, came ouit immediately before the last election campaign. I do not know whether it was made prominent diming the campaign or not, but this I 'do know, that the Minister of Railways and his colleagues this afternoon have pointed out that this railway construction into this wonderful portion of the Dominion of Canada which awaits development would cost the country approximately $13,000,000. That is one aspect of it only. That would give that country a railway connection with the present Canadian National system. Go a step further, and the expenditure of $20,000,000 would take the traffic through the Peace river pass, connect up with the Canadian National, and on to Prince Rupert and the Pacific ocean. My hon. friend the Minister of Health (Mr. King) goes further than that. He looks upon the completion of this great work as something that will ultimately have to be undertaken. If we go ahead with the project at all, it may in the end cost forty or fifty or sixty million dollars-that is, for a completed railway system through the Peace river district to the -coast.

Eighty-one million
dollars.

That is the maximum of expenditure. That is not a matter to be undertaken at a single jump. It will have to be undertaken as occasion requires, but the start should be made now, and a very substantial start; and very substantial relief may be given by the expenditure either of $13,000,000 or of $20,000,000. We do not seem to

Peace River Railway

have any very great difficulty in financing railway projects in other parts of Canada. We seem to be able to get three or four or five million dollars to build hotels for our railway system either in Paris or at Vancouver or some other point in Canada. It seems to give us no trouble whatever to do that. If we want eight or ten or twelve million dollars to improve our transportation facilities by way of developing harbours and building canals, we have no trouble whatever in getting the money. Now, what does this particular project, putting it at $20,000,000 as a maximum for the present, involve? It involves a loan of $20,000,000. Assuming the rate of interest to be five per cent, that is $1,000,000 a year. That is the total burden to this Dominion in respect of this development, and if the stories we have heard this afternoon and on other occasions of the wonderful possibilities of the Peace river district are true only to the extent of twenty-five per cent of the statements made, then the investment is a justifiable investment, one which the government should undertake in the interests of Canada and undertake at the present session, on account of the pledge of the Prime Minister of this country that it would be done.
I am glad, however, that the ministers have seen some new light during the course of the afternoon. They do not want this question to come to a vote now. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways is reluctant to condemn this project by a vote now. The government seem to think perhaps they can shelve the matter better by allowing it to come before a select or a special committee of this House. I am not opposing the suggestion.

Surely my hon. friend
understands that the suggestion came from his own colleague.

I know where it came
from; most good suggestions do come from this side of the House. I am not opposed to the suggestion, but I think the duty of the government and the duty of the Minister of Railways in this instance is to come to parliament and say:	Yes, the Prime Minister of
Canada did pledge the construction of this railway prior to the last election, and we are here to carry out that pledge.
These are the only remarks I have to make, Mr. Speaker, upon the subject. I think when the matter comes to the committee such a case will be made that the government will not be able to resist this construction that is demanded in the interests of the whole country-a work that should be proceeded with, with as little delay as possible.

Lest I forget, let me say at once that I agree with the suggestion that this matter be referred to the railway committee.
