I am inclined to that view because of the fact that there is a mass of evidence even in this report itself, a lot of which I cannot agree with, and which I should like to thresh out with the engineers as well as some others.
I am exceedingly gratified by the reception of this motion this afternoon. There are, however, a few things I wish to deal with, and I shall be as brief as possible because of the fact that we seem to be agreed on sending it to the committee.
The present Peace river country, the producing part of the country, consists of Grande Prairie, Pouce Coupe, the Spirit river settlement north of the Peace, and the High Prairie settlement. The Grande Prairie settlement needs approximately another fifty miles of railway to give it a branch line service. North of the Peace, where I live, another fifteen miles of branch railway is required, and I submit that if this mileage is built, with an additional fifteen or twenty miles into the Pouce Coupe district, which is a thickly settled farming area, you would have sufficient territory to feed the main line running to the Pacific coast and also the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway. The constituency of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) is not any bigger than the Grande Prairie district alone, and it is less than half of the district to which I have referred. It is not any richer in soil, and does not get any more moisture, and yet it has produced in one year 15,000,000 bushels of wheat.
I think this report of the engineers is unfair because of the fact that they have taken possibly the worst five years in the history of Canada, when the Peace river country was developing, from 1919 to 1924. That was just before the Peace river country got into its stride so far as development is concerned. They have calculated that in these five years the average export tonnage would be approximately 35,000 tons. But they also say that the only thing to consider in estimating the cost of a road to the Pacific coast would be farm produce, for various reasons. Now the total tonnage of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway in that year, and three-quarters of that is accounted for by Peace river, actually comes very close to 175,000 tons, whereas the engineers figured that the maximum tonnage at that time would average only around 35,000 tons.

No, 48,000 tons.

Peace River Railway

They credited 35,000
tons to the Peace river country.

It is on page 13 of the
report.

Page 25 says, "Present,
35,000 tons; initial, 175,000 tons." The total amount of grain handled over the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway from 1919 onward, and three-quarters of that was from the Peace river country, was as follows:
Year	Tons
1919		 41,000
1920		 49,000
1921		 45,000
1922		 68.000
1923		 60,000
1924		 96,000
1925		 89,000
1926	(11 months)	 91,000
Those are the figures of the Bureau of Statistics. The grain tonnage handled by the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway-and this is chiefly tonnage from the Peace river district-ran from 41,000 tons in the year 1919 to 91,000 in 1926. The total revenue tonnage was 155,000 and in eleven months of 1926 it ran to 237,000. That is the basis of my contention that this report is not doing the Peace river country justice, and I do not think the engineers will contend that their prophecy so far as the Peace river country is concerned was optimistic enough. These engineers were sent up to find out the best route for the development of the Peace river country. They have said that the Obed route is the best route of all. The Minister of the Interior this afternoon said that the Stewart route was the proper route; therefore, we require further investigation, and when that investigation is completed, why, $50,000,000 or $70,000,000 will not be too great an expenditure for the development of Peace River. It is all very well to want facts, but surely we have already some facts on which to proceed. I do not want to see this thing go on as the Hudson Bay railway has been going-as a negro said, "Vestigate, and vestigate and neveT do anything." I think to-day we have a report on which action might be taken. I doubt very much if the Stewart route is superior to the Monkman route, because the Monkman route, depending on which point you take, cuts off from one hundred to six hundred miles between the central points of the various zones of the Peace river country and Prince Rupert and Vancouver as compared with the present route. The straight line mileage from any point you like in the Peace river country to Stewart is just about seventy-five miles
shorter than the straight line to Prince Rupert, and unless there is something in British Columbia to call for the extra mileage, a new line north of the present Canadian National, I doubt very much whether there would be any justification for building another line there at the present time, moreover, I think it would mean an indefinitely long delay.
So far as the Obed route is concerned, there is a little difficulty in connection with the report. The report says that if you build the line from Aggie on the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway it will cost $13,000,000, but to complete that route another sixty mile branch from Grande Prairie across the Smoky river, is required, and that will run the cost of the 250 or 260 miles up as high -as the 168 miles of the line through the Monkman pass to whatever point in British Columbia the line touches the Grand Trunk. This estimate is $16,000,000.
Regarding the north side of the Peace, there will have to be another railway built someday, just as the Edmonton-Dunvegan had to be built from McLennan, in two sections, one serving Spirit river and Grande Prairie, and the other going up to Peace River and Whitelaw. Any railway from the west will also require two branches from Hudson Hope eastward, one running north of the Peace river and one south.
I am willing that this resolution should be referred, with the evidence we -have in the matter, to the standing committee on railways and canals, and of course we hope that the matter will be taken up by the House when the committee reports and that we will get somewhere with the matter then. If -the motion is not referred to the committee, my purpose is of course to press the matter to a vote.

I understand the hon.
gentleman consents to the reference to the standing committee on railways and canals.
Yes.

The hon. gentleman cannot amend his own motion, so that the hon. member fo.r Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) or some other member will have to move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), that the following words be added at the end of the resolution:
And that the matter be referred to the select standing committee on railways and canals.

Is that a proper motion
to be placed at the end of a main motion?
Peace River Railway

Would it
not be proper for the hon. Minister of Railways to move the amendment himself?
He has already spoken.
I am. willing to do it but I cannot.

Could we
not get the support of one member of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
move it.
-Mr. SPEAKER:	The motion is:
'That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the commencement forthwith and the completion in the near future of a direct railway outlet from the Peace River country to the Pacific coast and that this matter be referred to the select standing committee od railways and canals.
Instead of the word "and" we might substitute the word "but"-but that this matter be referred to the committee on railways and canals.

As I understand the
language the House would be committed nevertheless to the comencement forthwith of the work, and I certainly do not want to be committed to the commencement forthwith of this work. I cannot see my way clear, as Minister of Railways, to recommend it to the House just now.

My understanding of the
motion as altered by the amendment is that the House is not committed, but that the whole question is referred to the standing committee on railways and canals.

I for one am absolutely against this resolution if it means that the House is to be committed to the terms of the resolution. With all due respect for your ruling, Mr. Speaker, unless your ruling stands in the place of the resolution itself I cannot support it. If the House passes this resolution now it puts itself on record as in favour of the terms of it. The amendment has only the effect of adding to the resolution. The resolution remains for the time being and the committee will proceed immediately to examine it. When it goes to the committee, the committee will deal with a resolution which has already been agreed to by the House. As I understand it, that is not what the Minister of Railways wants; therefore, I object to the resolution as drafted.

I understand Your Honour gave a ruling a moment ago that this resolution itself was being sent

to the committee for their consideration, not necessarily with the approval of the House but in order that the committee might have something to work on.

This motion expresses
only a pious wish. With the amendment, the House now directs that nothing shall be done in connection with the motion until the select standing committee on railways and canals has studied it and reported thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Still, Mr. Speaker, even a pious wish may be more than what the House intended. Would it not be better to put it in this form?
That in the opinion of this House the select standing committee on railways and canals should consider whether the time has arrived, and so forth, and that this resolution be referred to it.

Will the hon. minister
kindly draft his motion?

Mr. Speaker, I can remember several occasions when resolutions of this nature have been referred to select standing committees or to special committees in terms identical with those of the amendment now before the House. The question has never been raised heretofore that the House was thereupon committed to the principle of the resolution. I think we shall be adopting the usual procedure if we alow the resolution as amended to pass.

Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to give to a committee the right to state that it has more judgment than the whole House. It may be that it has; I am not quite sure that numbers .make for quality. 1 understand that the motion, if amended as proposed, would simply mean that the committee would study the whole question and report to the House, leaving it to the House to decide on the merits. I for one am prepared to use what little judgment I have, but I am not prepared to give a power of attorney to fifteen or twenty other gentlemen to decide what my judgment should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so long as everyone considers that this is not committing the House to the principle of the resolution I do not see any objection to the motion as amended.

No resolution can commit the House of Commons to any expenditure except through the instrumentality of the crown. As I said before, it is simply a pious wish. The resolution has been discussed by the House and is now merely referred to the select standing committee on railways and

Dissolution of Parliament
canals, whose duty it will be to report to the House after having carefully examined the subject matter of the resolution. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion as amended?
Carried.
Motion agreed to.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, no government should have the right to ask for a dissolution of parliament prior to completing the five-year term as provided in the British North America Act except when authorized to do so by a majority vote of the House.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, we have had a very
pleasant and profitable trip through the Peace river country, viewing the scenery and considering the possibilities of that section of the Dominion. The purpose of this resolution is to bring us back into this chamber to consider some of our proceedings here.
The resolution as worded would seem to be quite orthodox in some respects. That is, it asks for the opinion of this House; it also hints that something should be done by means of a majority vote. There is, of course, a feature of the resolution that might be looked upon by some as altogether unorthodox, in that it brings before us for consideration a certain point of procedure that has not been practised hitherto. But I am not so sure that that should cause any consternation among hon. gentlemen. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is not so very long since this House adopted a procedure at variance with a long-established custom in this House. At the very opening of this present session the Bouse agreed to violate an established tradition in selecting its Speaker, that it has observed since confederation. It has been the well-established custom in choosing the Speaker of this House to alternate between representatives of the two dominant races in this country, the English and the French. None of us felt very badly over the breaking of that old established custom; indeed we were all quite satisfied to have Your Honour occupy the position for the third consecutive parliament. So that if we violate an old established tradition by adopting this resolution it may cause no more consternation than our departure from precedent at the opening of this parliament.
I purpose considering this resolution in the light of the practice followed in the mother parliament as well as in this parliament. As
hon. members are aware, there is a marked similarity between the Canadian and the British form of government; in fact, they are so nearly akin that one may be said to have been copied almost entirely from the other. In Great Britain parliament is composed of the crown, represented by the King or Queen, and by the two houses of parliament, the Commons and the Lords. Our parliament is much along the same lines, the crown being represented by the governor general and the two houses of parliament by the Commons and the Senate. In the Imperial parliament we have what might be termed two arms, the executive and the legislative, the executive arm being represented by the crown on the one hand through the king in council, and the legislative by parliament. Similarly, we have the two arms of government, the executive represented by the crown through the governor in council, and the legislative by parliament.
Looking first at the British form of government, it is what is known as a limited monarchy. It was not always so. Let me go back a few hundred years in order to establish the fact in our minds that there has been a gradual and noticeable change in the power and prerogatives of the British sovereign. Going back to the time of William the Conqueror, starting with the year 1085, we find that the crown at that time was almost absolute. In fact, the sovereign of that day had assumed the role of practically an absolute monarch in his ruling powers. Then, proceeding for a period of about one hundred and thirty years, up to the time of King John, the crown continued to exercise a very considerable power. But we know that in the year 1215 the people, as represented in what might be termed parliament, made demands upon King John and secured from an unwilling sovereign certain rights embodied in what we know as the Magna Charta. These rights may be said to have formed the foundation of British parliamentary government in Britain. Following that period, up to about 1485, the crown was more or less arbitrary in the exercise of its power. It seemed to assert itself and to predominate over the rights of the people as represented in parliament. Under the house of Tudor,, from 1485 until the year 1603, the crown continued to hold great power. As a matter of fact, in Henry VIII we find an almost absolute monarch of the type of William the Con- queror. Under the Stuarts, however, from 1603 to 1688 parliament made great constitutional progress. In the latter year the people, through their representatives in par-
Dissolution oj Parliament

Lament, drew up a declaration of rights which may be said to have inaugurated the prerogative of parliament and to have asserted the rights of that body over the crown.
The constitution of Britain now is not only that of a limited monarchy; it is largely an unwritten constitution. Now, this is quite in contrast with the situation that exists, for example, in the country to the south of us where we find a written constitution. When we speak of the British constitution being unwritten we mean that certain traditions are followed and certain practices established apart from any direct written authority. These traditions and precedents have come down to us and we have heard them referred to in this chamber quite often as established practices followed by the mother of parliaments.
In the British government the power is vested nominally in the crown, but that power is delegated practically to the cabinet. The power of the crown virtually rests in the cabinet, which is a committee of the legislative body. The cabinet is nominated by the crown. That is to say, the prime minister is nominated by the king and the cabinet by the prime minister in conjunction with the crown. It is safe, therefore, to say that the cabinet is nominated by the crown although dependent for its support upon parliament. In Britain the cabinet has the power of advising the dissolution of the assembly which it represents. The prime minister is, of course, the spokesman for the cabinet. There is a fine point here as to whether the prime minister has the absolute right to go to the crown and ask for a dissolution of parliament regardless of the wishes of his cabinet. It may be conceded that he has that right; I am not prepared to argue the point. Whether he has it or not, however, is a question that does not relate to this resolution now before the House. But it is a recognized fact that the prime minister has no legal primacy over the members of the cabinet. In fact it is only a matter of less than fifty years ago since the term "prime minister" was first used in any European document. In 1878 the term was first recognized in Britain, and it is only about twenty-two years now since the official precedence of the prime minister was first established in Britain.
As regards the power of the cabinet in the advising of a dissolution I purpose tracing in short form what has actually happened in Britain in the last twenty years. Let us take the history of the British parliament since the year 1906 up to the present date. We find that on February 13, 1906, parliament met,

dissolving on January 10, 1910, after an existence of three years, eleven months and twenty-four days, notwithstanding that the statutes of Great Britain call for a parliament of five years as a maximum. The next parliament assembled on February IS, 1910, was dissolved on November 28, 1910, having lasted nine months and thirteen days. The next one was called on January 31, 1911, and lasted until November 25, 1918, having been in existence for a period of seven years, nine months and twenty-five days. That was of course the war parliament, and that accounts for its having extended its life beyond the five year period. The next parliament was called on February 4, 1919, and was dissolved on October 26, 1922, so that it lasted for a period of three years, eight months and twenty-two days. The next one was called on November 20, 1922, and dissolved on November 16, 1923, after having sat for eleven months and twenty-seven days. The next parliament met on January 8, 1924; on October 9, 1924, it was dissolved, so that its life had not been more than nine months and one day. And the present parliament was called on December 2, 1924.
So that in a period of twenty years in Great Britain there have been seven parliaments, although the Parliament Act of 1911 stipulated that parliament should last for a period of five years. If we deduct the length of the parliament that carried on during the war, which existed altogether for seven years, almost eight years, we find that there have been six parliaments in the old land within a period of about twelve years, with an average life of two years each. One of these parliaments lasted only nine months and one day, while three of them existed for less than a year. This demonstrates the fact that, because of the power resting in the cabinet to dissolve parliament, the life of the legislative body is precarious indeed, and may be terminated at any time. In the old country, as we see, there have been a number of parliaments of very short duration.
I have not inquired into the cause of dissolution of each individual parliament, with a view to ascertaining whether in any case it was necessary or not; I was not particularly concerned with that point. What I wished to show was that under the British constitution parliaments have been rather short, three of them having been exceptionally so. This is a matter which might be regarded by some people as of little consequence, but when we consider the expenses inseparable from, a general election in a country like Great Britain we are bound to concede, I think, that it is of considerable moment. The expense of general elections, holding them every two

Dissolution of Parliament
yeans rather than every five years, is quite a strain, on the countiy. Under the British constitution the sovereign can dissolve parliament at his will, and no parliament can be assembled, prorogued, or dissolved without his express command. This resolution does not propose to invade that territory at all; the sovereign has that prerogative and so far as this resolution goes he has a perfect right to keep it.
Now let us look at our Canadian constitution for a short time. Without going into Canadian history too deeply, we should remind ourselves that here has been a struggle in Canada for constitutional reform and liberty and responsible government almost on a par with that in the old country. If we take the period of Canadian history from its earliest time up to the present we see that there has been quite a continuous struggle for responsible, representative government. In our early days we had a period of military government, almost a despotic government similar to the early days of British history, gradually the parliamentary institutions gained under such measures as the Quebec Act of 1774 and the Constitutional Act of 1791, but even these measures did not bring to the people all they wished. As a result in 1837 we had quite a decided uprising in both Upper and Lower Canada in favour of responsible government. The Act of Union of 1840 brought us a little further on the way, and then in 1867 the British North America Act was passed, of which I am sure we have all heard many times.
The British North America Act is supposed to be the great act upon which our constitution is based, and we are continually referred to that act as embodying certain rights and certain privileges which we hold and cherish very dearly. In section 50 of that act we have these wrords:
Every House of Commons shall continue for five years from the day of the return of the writs for choosing the House (subject to be sooner dissolved by the Governor general), and no longer.
That is one part of the British North America Act which we wish to consider more particularly. Provision is made that parliament shall last for a period of five years, unless sooner dissolved by the Governor General. You will notice that the act does not say "Governor General in Council"; it is the crown. That is, in Canada as in Great Britain, the crown has the right to dissolve parliament. I believe that is what was intended at the Imperial conference of 1926, since on page 14 of the proceedings we find these words:	(
In our opinion it is an essential consequence of the equality of status existing among the members of the British Commonwealth of Nations, that the Governor General of a dominion is the representative of the crown, holding in all essential respects the same position in relation to the administration of public affairs in the dominion as is held by His Majesty the King in Great Britain-[DOT]
Therefore it would appear to be the sense of the Imperial conference that the Governor General is the representative of the crown, and a^such he has the prerogative of dissolving the House. This resolution does not aim at taking away any such powers from the Governor General of Canada; there is no hint that that should be done. This resolution states that no government should have the right to ask for dissolution; in other words, the House of Commons should be supreme in these matters.
If we look at our Dominion parliaments since confederation we find quite a variation in their duration. From July 1, 1867, up to and including this present parliament, a period of sixty years, we have had sixteen instead of twelve parliaments, and during that time at least one of our parliaments extended over the five year period, while a great many did not last that long. I have a list here showing the duration of the different parliaments; they vary from ten months to six years, two months and seven days. Dissolution of Parliament

I would point out, however, that the last parliament began on September 5, 1925, and lasted until July, 1926, a period of about ten months. I do not propose to go into the whys and wherefores of the dissolutions of our Canadian parliaments; some hon. members might consider a dissolution justifiable, while others might think to the contrary. I simply point out the actual situation, that our parliament is dissolved prior to the completion of the term provided for in the act which is the foundation of our constitution.
It must be remembered also that dissolution takes place because a committee of this House decides that it should be done. It may bo that the Prime Minister of himself has that prerogative; I am not prepared to argue thar, but I hardly think the present Prime Minister has ever asked for dissolution without consulting his colleagues in the government. If he has done so he has done with his colleagues what he has not generally done in this House; for 'he has usually consulted the members of this House to ascertain the best procedure. Last session, of course, found us in a very unusual situation. We had a governing body without a majority in the House, and perhaps that has given rise to what might be termed a need for such a provision as that provided by this resolution. That is, where there is a government without a majority in the House it is an altogether different situation from a government with a strong following. I am prepared to grant that if the government had a following of two-thirds of the House, this resolution would not have so much force or effect, because such a government could easily carry a resolution to dissolve parliament. But when we have, as we had last session, a group carrying on which is less than one-half of the total membership of the House, the situation is quite different. Their legislation is brought in ordinarily with a sort of club held over their own following, and indeed in the last parliament held over some of the independent members, in that if legislation were not accepted, the government would dissolve the House and go to the country. That is rather an unfortunate situation.
Many hon. members, at least the independent members in this House, are more concerned about legislation than about dissolution or general elections, although none of us is so very anxious for a dissolution right away. We have had to run enough elections in the recent past to last us for a few years to come. We are more concerned about legislation, and we would like to consider legislation on its merits. When a legislative program is brought in or when a particular legislative proposal is made before the House,

we do not like to have that club held over us-you have to support the government or you will defeat the government, and if you defeat the government, that means another general election. That was the situation in the last parliament and I am not so sure that we are very far removed from it in this parliament. Oh, yes, we have a large number of members sitting on the other side of the chamber, but there is a ribbonlike row extending along there with a double row of defence ahead of them and a double row of defence behind them, and I am not so sure that row is one hundred per cent affiliated with the Liberal party. In fact, if we are to take at face value a statement that was made in this House in the early part of the session, the group to which I refer, strung along in that ribbonlike fashion, is organized as a separate entity with a chairman and a secretary and does not meet with the Liberal party in caucus. That situation has a very serious aspect. It means that the Liberal party has not a majority in the House, notwithstanding the fact that the press of this country has tried to lead us to believe that we now have stable government. I am not so sure that it is any more stable than it was in the last parliament, except that there are a few more to tend toward stability, but not enough to make it stable. That being the case, it is easy to conceive that during this very session of parliament legislation may be brought forward which will make it very unprofitable for some of that ribbonlike row in the centre of the group opposite us.

Another reason why it seems very necessary that some such provision as this should be made against dissolution is the fact that whatever party is in power, I care not whether it is the Liberal party or the Conservative party, there is a tendency on the part of such party to bring about dissolution at a very opportune time for that party, and the legislative program is shaped largely with that thought in view. Now we are going to go to the country and we must get a program that will appeal to the people. I am not going to say that that was what done last year. I do not know whether it was or not. I know the program was very appealing, but I am not going to say that that program was provided especially for going to the country on, but it does often happen that a government brings in a program that is especially appealing, and without any particular desire to get that program enacted into statutory legislation, they hie themselves to the country at their own sweet will and pleasure and bring on a general election, knowing that such a program will work in their own best interests. Mr. Speaker, such is not in the best interests of this country or of any other country. The expenses of a general election are no inconsiderable sum. The country is put to a great deal of expense, and individual members are put to a great deal of expense; business conditions are disrupted from one end of the country to the other, and on the whole a general election has a disturbing effect on the whole country.
I commend this resolution to this Chamber. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this House of Commons should be supreme in the matter of dissolution. No Prime Minister, and no cabinet, which is simply a body representing this chamber, should have the prerogative of going to His Excellency prior to the completion of the necessary five year term and saying: We must dissolve parliament. The cabinet is but a committee of this House, and, if you please, I would like to consider them as the servants of this House. That may not be a very dignified term to apply to them, but this House itself is but the servant of the nine million people of the Dominion of Canada. But the situation that existed in the last parliament, and exists in this so far as membership and groups are concerned, is altogether different from the condition that prevailed some years ago, and one that is going to exist for a few years to come. We are not going to get rid of the independent groups in this House just because some party men would like to get rid of them; they are here to-day and will be here for some time. In fact, if we compare the membership of the independent groups this year with last, counting the thin red line as being an independent group, we have more members in the independent ranks this year than last. So the independent groups are not dying out and that has given rise to a situation altogether different from what we had in this countiy sixty or a hundred years ago. The need, therefore, is apparent for considering the present situation.
I commend this resolution to the House. I am quite sure that if adopted it will not disturb our equilibrium in this chamber any more than the breaking of the old tradition of electing our Speaker. I am quite sure, too, that the adoption of this resolution will not disturb business conditions throughout the country or impede the wheels of industry one whit. On the other hand, I am sure that it will work to considerable advantage in the future.

Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution is indeed a very important one, and1 I am pleased to congratulate my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) on the way he has dealt with it. He has made a very interesting speech. I am sorry, however, to be compelled to confess that he has not convinced me that the British system in this matter is wrong. Under the British constitution, and this point my hon. friend has not touched at all, the underlying principle is that the country and parliament must be in harmony; they should not be at

variance. It sometimes happens-it has happened in the past both in Great Britain and in Canadh

that some parliament is elected in a ,period of patriotic exaltation or some other feeling, and a year or two afterwards it is perceived that it does not represent the majority of the people who voted' for it at the previous general election. It is necessary that at such a time a government should not be bound by a fixed rule compelling them to wait three or four more years before appealing to the people and allowing them to elect representatives who would more fairly represent the opinions and views of the majority of the people at that time.
True, as my hon. friend says, if his resolution were adopted a majority of parliament would be required before dissolution could be obtained, but that is just where the objection comes in; that is the obstacle. A House of Commons elected at a certain period would have a majority in the House to oppose dissolution later on at a time when the government considered dissolution necessary under the British constitutional system.

May I ask him to proceed from that point, and let us know the next step. How are you going to get out of that situation?

It has happened in the past, and I am going to quote instances. It is easy to perceive when a parliament is no longer in harmony with the people who elected them. You can see that especially when a series of by-elections goes against the government. That happened in England during Mr. Gladstone's time, in 1873 and 1875, and Mr. Gladstone went to the country two yeans before the expiration of his term of office just for that very reason. I quoted some words of his in a previous debate in the parliament that expired in 1921. Mr. Gladstone went to the country because all the by-elections were going against his government. He dissolved parliament, and in the general election that followed, he was defeated by an overwhelming majority, showing that he used good judgment in advising the crown to dissolve parliament. He was blamed for doing so at the following session. One of his previous supporters moved a resolution of censure against his course in dissolving parliament before the expiration of the term,

Dissolution oj Parliament
and in reply Mr. Gladstone said-British Parliamentary Debates, 1874, page 80:
My hon. friend seems to think that there is but one important element in the position of a government, and that is the numerical amount of its majority. Now, upon that -point I join issue with my hon. friend. I think he fundamentally misunderstands the constitution of this country if he supposes that the actual majority that a government may possess in an existing House of Commons is sufficient to give it more moral and political strength for the discharge of its arduous duties, after it has become apparent or when it is becoming clear that the possession of that majority is not agreeable to the sense and the convictions of the country. Now, Sir, there is the whole difference between my hon. friend and myself.
And he adds:
Because in this country we watch the signs and currents of public opinion. We recognize the general title of the country to be governed in conformity with its wishes and its intelligence; and the mere possession of a parliamentary majority, satisfactory as it is when it is a true indication of the actual current of feeling and opinion of the country, is no adequate support and no adequate warrant for the continuance of a government in office if it has become clear, or when there is reasonable ground for supposing, that the desires of the country are in an opposite direction.
In 1900 hon. gentlemen will remember that there was a khaki election. That was following the South African war, and two or three years after that election the government then in power met the same fate that the Gladstone government suffered in 1873. All the by-elections went against the government and then the opposition of that time moved that there should be a dissolution of parliament, because the majority in parliament did not any longer represent the sentiment of the country, and here is what Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman said at page 71 of the British Hansard of 1905:
It is common for us to say, and it is true constitutionally, that the minister of the crown in this country is selected and appointed "because he is the man who commands a majority in the House of Commons. But what does that mean? It means that the command of the majority of the House represents the feeling of the country. The moment the House of Commons gets out of touch and harmony with the country, then that plea for retaining office dissolves; and the right hon. gentleman has no right to entrench himself behind the confidence and support of his friends here after it is known to all mankind and to himself, as well as to any of them, that he has lost the confidence of the country. When I say it is known to himself, it is obviously so, because, if he was not aware he had lost the confidence of the country, why should he show any reluctance to appeal to the country and immensely strengthen his position by securing a favourable verdict from it.
That position was also taken by Sir Edward Grey, now Viscount Grey, and it is the position also advocated by the various authors on the constitution of England, especially Anson, Dicey and Green, who are here quoted. My hon. friend says that governments should not ask for a dissolution because it is contrary to the supremacy of parliament, iand his words to that effect were applauded. I believe in the supremacy of parliament, but I believe that the supremacy of the people must be above that of parliament when parliament no longer represents the majority of the views of the country. In such a case I think parliament should disappear and a new parliament should replace lit which would be a mirror of the conditions of the country as they exist at the time.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext: I believe the group in this House which can command the support of the majority of the members should carry on the government, but subject to the condition that the people are willing to have that group carry on. If the people show in an unmistakable way that this government or any other government does not any longer command the confidence of the majority of the people, I think this is a good time for a dissolution of parliament, and that we should not wait, as they do under the other system, until there has been a certain lapse of time. I do not think the American system is better than our own in that regard, and of course it is not based on the same principle. The President of the United States is elected by the direct vote of the people for a certain period of time. He is a ruler in the real sense of the word, not only in name but in fact, and it may very well happen, as it has happened in the past, that after elections, which occur in the United States every year for a certain part either of the senate or the congress, that the president does not command a majority in one or other of the houses, but the president has to carry on for the whole time for which he has been elected. Our system is quite different from that, and I do not believe it is inferior to it. I think there is a great advantage in keeping parliament and the country in harmony.

speechtext:
May I mention other
circumstances in which I believe the present system is best? For instance, when a very important measure involving a radical change in the national policy is submitted to parliament it is important for the government of the day to have this power of appealing direct to the electorate. Take the case of the Home Rule bill introduced by Gladstone and rejected by the British parliament; was it not essential that his government should have the right to appeal from the verdict of parliament to the verdict of the people? I quote that case because Gladstone was defeated when he went to the country on it, and it shows how essential it is that a government should consult the electorate on an issue first raised in parliament and on which the electorate have not had an opportunity to pronounce judgment.
Then again, take the case of Mr. Bonar Law. My friend referred to the fact that there had been three elections in Great Britain within three years, which he thought a calamity. Why? Mr. Bonar Law appealed to the electors on a policy of preference within the Empire. He had not been elected on such a program, and he thought he could not force through the House of Commons an issue on which the electorate had not been consulted. I think he took the only stand which a constitutional leader in a democratic country should take-not only to consult his own followers in parliament on a question which had not been debated and decided by the electorate, but also to dissolve parliament and go to the country. I think my view of the matter is at least as democratic as that of my friend. I think it is really the people whom I want to consult in such a case, and who under the British constitutional system of government are consulted. Mr. Bonar Law was defeated, but his action shows that he had a proper respect for the will of the electors. As a result of that election three parties were returned in almost equal proportions. Naturally it made government very difficult for some time. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, who had the largest group, carried on for a year, but finally he was defeated in the House of Commons. Surely then it was to the advantage of the United Kingdom that the electors should be given an opportunity to decide on what party should be returned to power They did decide. I do not know whether I was greatly pleased because a Conservative government was elected there, but they

secured a fair working majority, and since that time they seem to have had a reasonable degree of peace in England.

speechtext: Strange!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
Perhaps. Conditions
differ. May I mention one or two other circumstances where it is important that the government have the prerogative of dissolution? This has happened in Canada and in other countries. Under special circumstances, during a war for instance, a government goes to the country and is returned with a special mandate. When that mandate is fulfilled is it not better that the people should have the-opportunity of electing a new parliament on whatever issues may then be before the country? In countries where the franchise has been extended gradually from time to time, when the electorate is considerably enlarged or modified, is not that also a good reason for appealing to the new electors and giving them an opportunity to exercise the franchise?
I believe that the present system is the really democratic one and that there is no reason for changing it. My friend said that it is a tradition or a custom, and that we ourselves this session have broken a custom by electing you, Mr. Speaker, to the chair for a third consecutive term. But the subject we are discussing is more than a custom, a practice, a tradition. I submit, Sir, that it is the very basic principle on which our constitution is founded, and which makes it different from the American system of government. I am glad that this subject has come up for discussion. I know that many people think the change suggested by my hon. friend would be a good one. I repeat that I do not agree with that view, and that I think we should retain the system which is in force today.
May I conclude by reminding my hon. friend who has referred to the fact that this government is not any more stable than that which carried on last session, that I think it is more stable because we have a Forke in the present government!

He has based his argument in defence of the present practice on his respect for the people as being above parliament. Would he consider that a prime minister had a proper respect for the will of the people if at any time he should use his right to dissolve parliament as a club over the heads of hon. members?

That power could be
used as a club only if the prime minister has
a secure majority in the country. A prime minister who is weak, who cannot carry his elections, who does not feel that he is backed up and supported by a majority of the people would not use that club; the club would be used against him.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) must be congratulated upon having brought this subject before the House. No doubt for many years past, but especially during the last two or three years, an increasing number of people in the country have been asking themselves whether everything is right with our parliamentary system of government, and particularly whether the power of dissolution is always exercised in the best interests of the Dominion. It seems to me that instead of looking through books to find precedents and to discover what was done in this or that year in Great Britain or in this or that other country, we should devote ourselves more to this question: What is the system best suited to the needs of Canada now and in the near future? Of course, there is a good deal that may safely be borrowed from outside. I would be the last one to advise my compatriots and the members of this parliament to disregard all British precedents. But if I understand my British history, and with the little knowledge I have of the British parliamentary system of government, I am bound to say this, that precedent after precedent has -been established to meet at particular times the needs of the people of the British Isles, now Great Britain. And if we are so concerned about imitating the British people in -the operation of their system, we should do what they are doing and apply ourselves to find out in what respects their system -corresponds to our needs and to our situation -generally, and in what directions we should make changes as they are needed. I -have never considered- it necessary to show our admiration for the British people and their -constitution by making ourselves monkey-like British subjects and copying everything done in Great Britain simply because it is done in Great Britain. For example, I have never been -able -to bring myself to the point of turning up the bottom of my trouser legs simply because it is raining in London. The conditions in Canada, -geographical, political and economic, are i-n many -respects different from those in Great Britain. In -many respects -they are -certainly -much more similar to the -conditions that prevail in -the United States. So t-hat before we declare outright that -the Americans are all
Dissolution of Parliament

wrong in their method of dealing with political problems, and go on following mechanically what is done in Great Britain, we should consider conditions in their 'bearing on the various aspects of the question.
The first thing to be considered is, in my opinion, the question of the relations that exist or that should exist between the executive and the legislative power. This has been a great subject of dispute and the occasion for many precedents that have displaced each other in Great Britain from * time immemorial. Indeed, the makers of the American constitution decided upon a separation between the executive and the legislative powers in the United States precisely because of their deep knowledge of British history and because they wanted to avoid, in the operation of political powers in the United States, such difficulties as had arisen in Great Britain and had from time to time brought into conflict the king and the lords, the lords and the commons, or the king and parliament at large. And it is precisely because, on the one hand, they wanted to strengthen the hand of the executive power in. the management of the general affairs of the country, and on the other, to reserve to the legislative body that full independence derived from the mandate given by the people, that they decided to make the executive absolutely independent for the four years during which it should be in power, and at the same time guarantee to the legislative power complete independence in relation .to the legislative measures it adopted as well as in the votes which it might give on the budget of the country. On the whole, I do not think it has worked so badly; and before discarding altogether that American precedent, which is nothing else than the result of many centuries of British precedents, or the putting into .concrete form of the thought, or the maturation of thought of many British legislators and British jurists, we should question seriously the wisdom of copying what was done by Lord Beaconsfield or Mr. Gladstone in this year or that year. Rather, we should ask ourselves whether, our conditions being more like those that obtain in the United States, we should not to a certain extent combine in our own system of government something of British precedent and something of American practice.
As to the rights of the people and their supremacy, and the rights of democracy, all that of course sounds very well. All parties, all leaders, all representatives of the people pay a tremendous amount of respect to the

voters so long as they think they can win their votes.. And in our own history, as well as in the history of Great Britain, it has been proved that once entrenched in power governments have all more or less respected the will of the people. This applies even to that great statesman, Disraeli, who after having fought the popular will, both on the Corn Law and in connection with the Reform laws, discovering that he was likely to lose in the end, risked the support of the landed gentry on his Tory policy, turned his coat, and adopted a more radical policy than that of the Liberal party, which he had previously opposed. This he explained by saying that his party had educated their masters.
The point, is not whether public opinion as expressed by the votes of the people will be supreme in the long run. That is admitted. The question is, what is the most practical means by which an elected parliament will carry on the government of the country for the normal period for which it has been returned, and keep a proper balance between the democratic principle and the maintenance of a government which will respect itself, respect the House and respect the people. I quite admit with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that if a great unforeseen question arises during the lifetime of a parliament, if the government, faced with the necessity of taking a stand on such a question, finds either through the House or from outside expressions of opinion that it cannot exercise its responsibilities and pass legislation on that question, it should ask for a dissolution in order to obtain a fresh mandate from the people on that particular matter. Such questions do arise once in a while, but they are rather infrequent. The other aspect of the question raised by several gentlemen on the opposite side presents itself at almost every session. The government brings down legislation which may be in the interests of the people, but which is imposed upon them by certain groups or large interests. If a portion of the majority is unwilling to accept such legislation by conviction, the ministers turn to those members and say, " Well, we are bound to bring it down, and if you do not accept it we will dissolve parliament." This is another aspect, a smaller one I admit but one which must not be disregarded; because, after all, the public life of a country, the standard of public morality and the public spirit are not to be measured by the attitude of parliament or of the people upon great or rare occasions, but by the daily life of the countiy and parliament; and everything which makes for the greater independence of parliament makes for the greater liberty of the people.

Dissolution oj Parliament
On the other hand I must say that I was quite shocked to hear the hon. gentleman asking this House to say that the majority shall decide whether or not dissolution could be granted. If this resolution were voted in this form it would simply strengthen the hands of a powerful and unscrupulous government to enforce upon the weak and timeserving majority that very dangerous power against which we are both protesting. The stronger and more unscrupulous the government, the more time-serving will be the majority at the back of that government, and if this resolution is voted where is the remedy?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean that if the government have a strong following in the House they would be sustained and would not be granted a dissolution?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
My argument is that
under the holy rule of democracy the more unscrupulous the government, the stronger it is with the people and with parliament. I must say that I have not much faith in democracy, in spite of all the millions we have spent to make it reign all over the world. Let us leave that for a moment, however, and turn back to something else. You have a government with a large number of followers interested individually in not going to the people, in not running the risk of an election. If the legislation proposed is unpopular and against the interests of the people but must be swallowed up for certain considerations, it is generally brought in at the beginning of a parliament. I have sat in this House in the olden times; I have studied the records of this parliament, and the more shameful a policy, the more detrimental it is to the interests of the people, the more generally it has been brought in by a strong government with a strong majority at the beginning of parliament. That has happened with all parties and if some of the followers said, "We cannot swallow that", the government replied, "Well, my good fellows, if you do not swallow it you will have to go to the people; if you do not stand by the government, will you stand by the opposition which you have fought? We have supplied you with electoral funds; where else will you get your moral help to convince the consciences of the people?" The result is that the stronger the government and the larger its majority, the greater is the tendency to impose any kind of legislation under threat of dissolution. Therefore I quite agree with the Minister of Justice, and I am quite sure my hon. friends opposite do not desire to bring this new-born democracy, with its feeble conscience, to the state of political morality which existed at the time of Disraeli and the
remnants of the pocket boroughs. If we want to have some kind of practical administration we must prepare something similar to what the Americans have done; give to the people the absolute right to decide on certain occasion who their representatives will be, and then stand by the consequences for the time being. It is far better to have elections at a fixed date than have dissolution upon any pretence; and I would further say that neither the Governor General, the Lieutenant Governor nor any other single gentleman, at Rideau Hall or elsewhere, a man not representative of the people, should have that right; I will never stand for that. I would say that power should be reserved to the executive chosen by the majority of the House, and possessing the confidence of the House.
On any trivial matter, any measure which ma3r be brought in by this or that minister, the House should be free to accept or refuse it, and let the government abide by the decision of the House. The people do not ask to be consulted in a general election upon any trifling bill which may be brought in by the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Railways or anyone else; the people are more reasonable than they are sometimes represented. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has well said, they want to be consulted upon great measures of unforeseen consequences. For example, I know the people in my province felt indignant when this parliament, which had been elected on certain matters of administration, decided by an understanding reached between the two parties that we should go to war in Europe. That feeling of indignation spread all over the country, when the constitution of this country was violated to permit Liberals and Conservatives to sit for one year more than they had been elected for, in order to impose conscription on the people. Yes, the people feel indignant at these violations not only of British precedents, but of the most elementary rights of justice and common sense.
But if a minister proposes that a grant of money be made to build the Peace river railway or any other railway; if a minister brings in a measure for the administration of his department, let the House decide whether or not such a measure shall be supported or such a grant of money be voted. It is not necessary to disturb the business of the country and dissolve parliament for that. If the minister concerned considers that he is no longer able to fill his position in the cabinet, let him resign, something which is done frequently not only in France and other countries, but in Great Britain as well. I have not the precedents in mind at the

speechtext:
My hon. friend will find out in a few years whether Ramsay MacDonald is killed or not. That is the game of party, as we all understand. In every country that brand of politics is to be found. They are no better or worse in Great Britain than we are here; we should not be either proud or ashamed of the difference. There is just about the same human nature everywhere. But evidently they discovered and they now know that the thinking and working democracy of Great Britain is tired of being appealed to from morth to month by time-serving politicians.
Likewise, the people of Canada, do not care to have such frequent elections. The people who realty consider and value their citizenship do not care to be called upon every six months or every year to pass through the turmoil of general elections. What they care about is that the men andi parties that appeal to 'them, once elected and in parliament, should give them at least twenty-five per cent of their promises. The people are beginning to be more concerned about the results; and for that reason we should come to the point of combining the best part of the old traditional spirit of British government.,-which was not democratic, which was entirely and thoroughly aristocratic, which was based upon contempt for the people, which meant simply the selection of a few individuals by a somewhat larger

Dissolution of Parliament
number of individuals,-and the best part of the American system of government, which has its dangers, which threatens not only the American people but the world1 at large with the domination of plutocracy taking the place of the old landed! gentry which governed England, but which nevertheless offers some examples that we might make use of.
Gan we not have faith in ourselves, I will not say in our genius, but simply in our common sense, to try to adapt to our conditions such measures or systems of government which may or may not exist elsewhere, without asking ourselves: Has that been borne and brought up under the British flag? Does this bear the English or the French stamp? Let us endeavour to build something by ourselves out of our own comlmon sense, taking advantage of course of what is good and what has produced good elsewhere, endeavouring also to avoid the dangers and the clap-traps into which other countries have fallen. If we do that, it will be quite possible to devise a system which will not prevent any majority from declaring that the government has lost its confidence and should go to the people. I would! keep that part of the British precedent, because that, instead of being a club in the hands of ten men against two hundred, would be a club in the hands of two hundred men against ten. It would be far more effective. I quite admit that it will take a long time before a truly party majority will make use of that cliub aigaimst its own government; but nevertheless, leave in the hands of a majority of the House to cteclare that tihe government has lost its confidence, and therefore that an appeal should be m&de to the people. I think this would meet the object of the motion of the hon. gentleman, as well as the object of the motion standing on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. 'Garland). Unless there is a decided vote given by the majority of the House to defeat the government and send it to the people, I claim that we should follow the American system and declare that the House shall not be dissolved until the expiration of the five years for which it is elected.
As regards the prerogatives of the Governor General, I hope that nobody and no group iu this House will stand up and ask us to go back on a principle which now stands unchallenged in every country where floats the British flag. I am not apt to wave the British flag, but I hope that gentlemen in this House who are prepared to wave it upon all occasions and sing "God Save the King" on every street corner, will be prepared to stand up here and say that in the House of Commons of Canada
we are not prepared to go one hundred and fifty years back of the people of Great Britain, back of the people of Australia, of New Zealand, and of every other country which acknowledges the British king as its sovereign. There is not a teacher of law, there is not a statesman, there is not a public man under the British flag in any other country but Canada, who would claim to-day that the king, or in any part of the king's dominions, the representative of the king, has the right to dissolve parliament unless it is by the advice of his legal counsellors.
I hope hon. gentlemen will forgive me a little heat upon that point. Of course, it is in the blood; but I 'hope also that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will realize that if I have taken a somewhat unexpected share in this debate it is because I earnestly hope that all men of goodwill will join hands to see that in the functioning of our representative institutions there shall be a growth, a development which will both satisfy the need which has been well presented by the hon. gentleman, and as to which a great many people in the country feel as he does and desire a remedy for that situation, and at the same time keep in view the principles which the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has laid down. It seems to me that this is a subject which might usefully occupy the minds of a few hon. gentlemen in some committee of the House. It would certainly be as useful and as timely a subject to engage their attention as the amendment of the rules of the House, which subject is to be brought before this body within a few days. There is no doubt that the people in the country feel uneasy at the uncertainty of government and of legislation. They feel that at times too much legislation is forced upon a weak government by some group holding in its hands the power to maintain or overthrow that government. They also feel that very often weak representatives of the people let a strong or daring government impose upon them legislation against their conscience and against the interests of the people they represent. We must have more freedom, we must have more order, and we must also have a little more businesslike spirit in the working of our institutions.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, I wish to add only a very few sentences to this very interesting and, to my mind, very important debate. I was not surprised that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) defended the present system, I have, as has been said by other members of this group, a very great respect

Dissolution of Parliament

for the Minister of Justice, but the people who benefit from a certain system are almost always found in the ranks of its defenders. .
If I understand the speech of the Minister of Justice the leading point in it was that the cabinet knew better than the members of the House of Commons what the people of the country wanted. As a matter of fact, I think they know much less about what the people want than do the members of the House of Commons, and for a very good reason; they have not the chance to know. I have said that before. When ministers go to their own constituencies there is such a terrific pow-wow made about them that they never happen to hear what the people are really thinking. They are welcomed everywhere with respect and a great show of elation and so they do not get to know, as we common individuals do, what are the people's thoughts on specific questions. I do not think there is any doubt about that, and I am amazed at the modesty of the Minister of Justice that he should stand up here and say that he and his colleagues in the cabinet know more about what the people in nine provinces want than do the representatives from the 245 constituencies. I think we must all admit, I think even the most partisan, even the most blind, must admit that a gradual but continuing change is coming over our form of government. Responsible government once meant being responsible to the crown. However, gradually a change has come about until responsible government to-day does not mean responsibility to the crown; it means responsibility to the people, and so the House of Commons, being the chamber in which the representatives of the people sit, is the most important part of the government of Canada or of Great Britain. If it is not, at least it ought to be, and to my mind it will not be so very long before the cabinet is what I once heard the Minister of Finance say in a previous parliament that it was-ra committee of the House of Commons. It is, of course, not that, but it ought to be, and I think as we become seized of the fact that responsible government does mean government responsible to the people, we will also come to know that a cabinet should be a committee that is responsible to the House of Commons; and if they are not responsible to the House of Commons, they are not useful, and there should be some way in which we can get rid of them.
I think everyone who has sat in this House knows that very many times government supporters are forced-I think that word is not too strong-into supporting measures for
IMiss Macphail.]
which they have no use at all, simply to avoid having their leader, the Prime Minister of the country, go and ask for a dissolution of parliament, and thereby bring upon our heads that which members of parliament dislike most, a general election. I recall, and I am sure you do, too, Mr. Speaker, the time when Mr. Andrew McMaster, then member for Brome, introduced a resolution that cabinet ministers should not hold directorships in great companies. I yet recall the sullen faces of the Liberal members when they were forced-I use that word advisedly -to vote against that resolution which they themselves, a very few months before had, almost all, if not all, supported.

Their masters had
educated them.
