speechtext: Yes. I remember some of them were so angry that we did not,see them in the chamber for some days afterwards. That sort of thing is bad for the character-yes, it is bad for their disposition, as my seatmate says, but it is bad for the character, and if they stay in the House of Commons and are continually put in a position where they must vote against their honest convictions, I am afraid they will cease-well, one hates to say it-to have honest convictions. The system of government that brings about a condition like that is a very bad system.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
It has been argued tonight by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, who spoke so eloquently and held us with such interest, that where a party had a majority in the House, if they voted together, they could at any time by a vote of the Commons bring about a dissolution. But we must admit-and I know that some members will do it with very great reluctance -that in Canada we are not as much wedded to the two-party system of government as we used to be, and that there are growing up in Canada economic groups-you can call them class groups if you like, because that is what they are-which are the result of an organization in the country. These groups come here to speak with the voice of a particular industry. I am one such. There are many of us in this corner of the House. We have no particular interest in party government. We do not care which party is the government. We care very much.what kind of legislation they offer us, but the name of the party itself is of no personal concern to us, and so it seems to me, as this thing con-

Dissolution oj Parliament
tinues-and I think there is no doubt it is going to continue-that some new way of carrying on government in this House must be found, and that a time will come-and surely this resolution is one step towards it- when members will be liberated and able to express their honest convictions. Of course it sounds revolutionary, but I do not think it is so dangerous. The time will come when members can vote on issues as they arise, whether they are government measures or not., and when they, the members of the House of Commons, believe that it is in the best interests of all the people to bring about a general election, my faith in the members of the House of Commons is sufficient to believe that they will bring about a general election, and are more likely to bring it about at a time when it is in the general interest and for the welfare of the general public than are a few men who are known as the members of the cabinet.
I do not intend to continue my speech, which is not really a speech. I entreat hon. members-I was going to say hon gentlemen; it- would be all right for me to say that, because so many of you say hon. gentlemen, but hon. members is a better expression-I entreat hon. members not to close their eyes to the fact that changes are taking place in Canada, first in the organization in the constituency. The old bluff stuff, even with lots of money behind it, does not work as it used to do. There is an organized electorate which has a collective intelligence and they are exercising it, and so we had better get rid of the old system, as the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa) said, and use our own common sense in the creation of a system that suits our own conditions. We can do it if we forget all the precedents that ever were.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
Unlike the
hon. lady from Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail), I was somewhat surprised at the stand the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) took against this proposed improvement in our methods of doing business in this House. I had usually associated the hon. member with a certain fine elasticity of mind and with a spirit that was attuned to democracy, but somehow or other the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Kennedy) must have caught the blind spot in his eye to-night. I was so much impressed with the speech of the hon. member that I thought it was worthy of at least my support. I am glad there are not many voices in this House-they seem to be a diminishing quantity-that are prepared to speak out on behalf of widening the elbow room in this chamber for Canadian democracy.
This power of cabinets to dissolve parliament is one of those vestigial things that come down to us not from times when men climbed trees but when certain classes of men found themselves up trees and sought an easy way to climb down. It is a curious thing that in the growth of our British constitution that power was wrested from the hands of autocracy and handed down to the people in very short stages. When they took this power from the monarch they did not place it immediately into the hands of the people, but placed it in the hands of the oligarchy, and there it has remained ever since to the detriment of democracy.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
That was Cromwell's
work.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
Like all things of this character that have outlived their usefulness, that time has caused to seem uncouth, it has become a kind of incubator of disease in the body politic. I feel sure myself that this power, remaining beyond its time, outgrowing its usefulness and purpose, has had a pernicious influence upon our government. It has provided a means whereby governments, oligarchies, small cliques of men, have been able to club popular assemblies into insensibility towards the wishes of the people. It is a sad thing, the influence that popular assemblies, so-called, have upon the members who from time to time are sent to them. It does not require very much to take the edge off those fine sentiments with which men first make their appearance in these assemblies. It does not take much, it seems, to dilute those high principles which animate our breast when first we make our entry into these places. One of the things that is most responsible for killing these enthusiasms, for destroying these attachments to high principles is the influence of the party whip. What is it that gives to the party whip his power, his torpedo-like effect upon the followers of a government? When he draws out the black snake and cracks it over the heads of his party's followers, then enthusiasms decay and evaporate. Why is it? Simply because we have allowed to survive into our age of democracy this vestige of times gone by when it may have had some use to buttress autocracy, but never to strengthen democracy.
I am sure that this out-of-date practice also fosters what I may call opportunism in government. This does not need very much fostering, because in times gone by it has been the very spirit of the politician. But here is something that deliberately fosters opportunism in government. It allows governments to lengthen their term of office-I am arguing
Dissolution of Parliament

contrary to the Minister of Justice; it is just as legitimate one way or the other-I say it permits governments to prolong their life until they think it is opportune to consult the people. Here we are in parliament supposed to be transacting the people's business, but from election to election we sit gazing out of the window wondering what kind of political weather it is going to be instead of transacting the people's business. We have our eye upon the political barometer. My hon. friend says that governments keep their eyes on by-elections, and that as the mercury rises or falls, it determines the length of life of governments. I may have made a mistake in checking up my hon. friend on the dates he mentions, but I remember that in 1874 when Gladstone went to the country because he felt that the political barometer was falling his government was succeeded by the Disraeli government, one of the most inept, retrograde, shallow and inefficient governments that ever held office in England. Throughout their term of office they scanned the political horizon and when they thought the barometer was rising-several by-elections went in their favour-they appealed to the country. What happened? They were severely beaten. The political barometer failed them, why should not it fail at any other time? In our own experience we know there has been such a failure. The political barometer proved to be misleading as recently as last session. What was it then that impelled the government of the day to go to the country but their sizing up of the political situation? You know, Mr. Speaker, as well as I do that not ten per cent of the people were wanting an election last year; they were wanting legislation, as the member for Southeast Grey said. Nevertheless they got an election, and they got it because of this outworn practice that we have saddled upon us in this democratic age. Here we have political parties watching the clouds. As the Scripture says, when you watch the clouds you do not sow. That is one reason why parliaments are so sterile in legislation-most of the time is spent between looking back to. the last election and forward to the next.
I think this custom is out of keeping with present-day parliamentary conditions. As the member for Southeast Grey said, the members of the older groups in this House have always deliberately refused to recognize the emergence of the third party. We are in the age of the multi-group system; groups have come to stay. The fact that the group I represent in this parliament sits partly on one side of the House and partly on the other does not, I think, make much difference. Person-

ally I feel sorry in a sense to see my colleagues sitting over on the other side of the chamber, but perhaps it is due from me to say to the House that it might be as well for those who do not understand the situation not to try to derive too much comfort from seeing some of my colleagues on the benches opposite. I think my colleagues there will agree with me that in the last five years, in Manitoba at any rate, there has been no fundamental change in the opinion of the people; they are not one whit more attached to the bi-party system to-day than they were in 1921. I say to my friends of both parties that if I were in their position I would not presume too much from the fact, regrettable enough to me, that some of my colleagues are sitting where they are to-night.
I want to say that it is an insult to the democratic spirit that has manifested itself throughout the country in the last six years to make almost deliberate attempts to disintegrate the third party both in this House and in the country. It cannot be done. There is such a momentum behind the movement that all this petty obstruction can have only a momentary effect. I would have been proud, indeed gratified, if the Minister of Justice speaking, as he presumably does, for the government, had assumed a more generous attitude towards this measure of reform that has been put before us to-night. I do not say that it is sufficient. I think possibly it has a serious defect.
I could not see very much difference between the position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) and that of the member for Ivindersley, except perhaps that one was a little more stringent than the other. After all, these things are but details in a wider system of renovation which is overdue in our Canadian parliament. Anyone who knows parliament, who has had experience of it, knows that out of all its turmoil, out of all its labours, there comes forth precious little in the way of advanced legislation for the benefit of the people. And why is that? Is it not reasonable to assume that it is because of the antiquated system to which we are clinging? From my own observation I am sure it is. Parliament is not functioning as it should function in a democratic country; the voice of the people is stifled the moment it tries to find expression in this House. The moment the will of the people tries to express itself, it is cribbed, cabined and confined in this very place which traditionally is supposed to stand for the rights of all. Why should any Liberal quarrel with a new and rising democracy? When this new spirit of democracy, this clamant call of the people
[DOT]293

Dissolution oj Parliament
for better representation, makes itself felt here, why should it be restrained? Why should it not be given every reasonable encouragement? Is not this the home of democratic institutions? This is the place that has been reared through generations to welcome the voice and the spirit of the people. We cannot therefore take this resolution lightly to-night. While it may be very inadequate, yet it points to something that is eating at the very vitals of our public life.
A few days ago I received from one of our outstanding newspapers a pamphlet aimed at converting me to the system of Mussolini in Italy. Why should an intelligently conducted journal try to foist that system on Canada? Because evidently it sees its opportunity; it sees some vital debility in the present system. But are we believers in British constitutional development going to listen to the wild, thoughtless, wrecking advice of a capitalistic newspaper and overturn the traditions of our beloved country simply because, being subsidized, that newspaper is able to pamphleteer us? Let us act like reasonable men and try to keep our constitutional development along the sound lines that have been laid down by our British statesmen in days gone by. Those men were not perfect; they shapd their policies to fit in ' with the needs and the state of devlopment in the time in which they lived. But their vision was far-reaching nevertheless.
I do not think we can take the speech of the Minister of Justice very seriously because, in my opinion at any rate, it represents no fundamental philosophy in his own mind. I would much rather believe that he is on the side of the angels with respect to these things; if he is not, he should be. In looking up a reference a short while ago, explaining why Gladstone became disheartened, went to the country, and finally retired from the leadership of his party, I found a very interesting passage. Mr. Chamberlain, who at that time was the strongest radical in British politics, was himself dragging Mr. Gladstone, Napoleon-like, into his Elba. Chamberlain advised the Liberals at that time to vote against the government of their party until they should learn the Liberal alphabet sufficiently well to be able to spell the first words of the Liberal cause. He repeated that throughout the length and breadth of England, with the result that the Liberal government was turned out of power. They had to learn the alphabet of liberalism. I do not think we heard the alphabet of liberalism to-night from the lips of the Minister of Justice. We heard a strange language, a foreign accent,-

And I say it sincerely, and not at all in any captious; spirit, because I am thoroughly convinced that what the minister said to-night was not inspired by anything he can find in the story of Liberalism. He will search in vain the lives of Liberal statesmen, he will read Liberal textbooks as much as he likes, he will find nothing at all in keeping with the spirit of the little address he gave us to-night.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
I do not propose at this late hour to go fully into this question, important though it is. I believe however that it is of sufficient importance to merit greater consideration than the House will be able to give it to-night. Unlike the previous speaker (Mr. Bird), I was rather impressed with the argument of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), although not with the whole of it. Certainly I think he presented the constitutional principle at its very best, and there is something well worth safeguarding in that principle. On the other hand, I should hope tha-t the Minister of Justice would be willing to admit that the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) is trying to remove from the practice of parliament something that is a real grievance and hindrance, both to democracy and to the best interests of the House. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has presented both sides of the question clearly to us. Judging from the remarks of the Minister of Justice it would be surprising to me if this resolution were to pass. I think his very utterance, under the present practice of parliament, draws to his support every member on the other side of the House who belongs to his party, and that being so the resolution will of course be lost. I believe, on the other hand, that if a committee were appointed to study the question, or if one of the standing committees were delegated to take it into consideration and discuss it, something might possibly develop which could be adopted. It is obvious to everyone that the chief thing we are trying to get away from in the resolution is the power which a prime minister wields in parliament by his continual threat to dissolve parliament if certain legislation is not passed. That is the most important point implied in the resolution. Therefore, in view of the importance of the resolution, and also in the
Dissolution of Parliament

hope that with greater or more mature consideration some means will be found whereby the principle set forth by the Minister of Justice, and the one emphasized by the hon. member for Kindersley, may be embodied in one practice, I move seconded by Mr. Spencer, that the resolution be amended by adding the words, "That this resolution be referred to the committee on rules of the House."

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
It is so seldom that I have an
opportunity of agreeing with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that even at this late hour I am not going to let the opportunity pass of saying that I do agree with him in the stand that he takes in regard to this resolution. The Minister of Justice stated that the will of the people was above even the will of parliament, and if that is so I would like to say that in the last election the party on this side of the House, of which 1 am a humble member, polled more of the popular vote than did the parties represented by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). Therefore, in so far as public opinion is concerned, I may find myself at variance with the minister.
I do not intend to take many minutes at this late hour to discuss this question. We have listened to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who has certainly a very extensive vocabulary and who does not, intend that any part of that vocabulary shall grow rusty through disuse. I will readily admit that he is a fluent and interesting speaker at all times; perhaps more interesting when you hear him first than when you hear him later on because of his frequent repetitions and all-embracing generalities which come up in almost every speech. If the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle had any meaning at all they meant in one part that we should adopt the cast iron, iron clad system of the United States. But apparently that did not suit him, nor did the motion of the hon. member for Kindersley please him. That is not unnatural with the hon. member for Labelle; in fact that is playing true to form, When has any person known the hon. member to agree with any person, any party, or any individual except the hon. member for Labelle?
I can easily understand the attitude of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) and the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), in their desire to hang on to their seats for five years, no matter what the circumstances are. When a person will cut short a trip across the Atlantic in order to try to keep in power a party which that

person has already denounced as unfit to hold the reigns of office; when a person will "inadvertently" cast his vote to keep that party in power, I can well understand the attitude of those hon. members this evening in saying that parliament should extend over the full term of five years no matter what the circumstances may be, in order that they may hold the seats which they now represent.
The hon. member for Labelle frequently pays tributes, in that tone of voice and attitude which generally characterize all his utterances, to the British constitution and British institutions, but he generally endeavours to find something with which he endeavours to discredit them afterwards. So he said, with that flourish not of trumpets but of arms, with that acrobatic performance which nearly always goes with his speeches in this House, "We must not accept British precedents and British practices because they are British." All I have to say, Mr. Speaker, and I say it to the hon. member for Labelle and need say it to no others in this House, that neither do we have to discard British practices and British precedents because they are British. I think we are on pretty safe ground in following the practice of the mother of parliaments in regard to this matter, as we might very well follow them in regard to many other matters, and as most ' of the civilized countries in the world have followed them also. I believe that our course here is far more democratic and more in conformity with the will of the people than is the practice across the line in the United States of America.
It was said by one of the speakers, if not by the hon. member for Labelle, that the government might use its power of dissolution as a threat or club over hon. members to force them into submission. That is not a practice which I will endorse or which should be endorsed, but I venture to submit that it is no worse for the government to do that, having on their shoulders the responsibility of carrying On government, than it was for the hon. member for Labelle to rise in his place in this House last session and convey to the government the threat that unless they changed certain legislation 'he would tell something that took place in a secret conference in 1905. Who was holding a club in that case? I do not think it any worse for the government to exercise its right of dissolution than it was for certain hon. gentlemen from the city of Winnipeg to exercise their power and authority in this House last session and say to the government, "Give us this legislation or give us that, or out you go." It may be that the government may see

Dissolution of Parliament
fit to dissolve parliament, but it seems to me that according to human nature as exemplified by this government, they are not very apt to dissolve parliament short of the legal term.
I think we can take it for granted that they will hang on as long as they possibly can, at least I am convinced that I have seen evidences to that effect on several occasions. But I can conceive that it may be possible for circumstances to arise in the country whereby a certain matter may come up which will agitate Canada from one end to the other, and where the government must take a firm stand.
I want to say here that I do not agree with the hon. member for Southeast Grey when she says that the ordinary member of parliament is in a better position to get public opinion than are members of the cabinet. I disagree with that absolutely, because it is the business of the cabinet, selected from all parts of the country, to make themselves familiar with public opinion on all great questions. If the government of the country take a stand on a question; they are a number of men bound together and acting together, and if certain other men take the opposite side on a question which is agitating the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, then I say it is right for the government to tell the others. "We believe we are right; we may be in the minority in the House, but we believe the people of the country are with us, and believing that we will submit this question to the people." In that case they should not be dictated to by a few individuals in this House representing any class or group who think they hold the upper hand and can force the government to do what they will.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, taking into consideration all these matters I am inclined to agree with the position taken by the Minister of Justice. I listened of course with attention and interest to the remarks made by hon. gentlemen and the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) in the southeast comer of the House, the Progressives. If democracy has been smashed to splinters in the opinion of those hon. members, if the liberties of the people are being violated and all that sort of thing, why do they not use their great influence in Manitoba and Alberta, where they have Progressive governments, and get. them to institute such a system out there? Have they done that? Not that I have heard.

speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
When?
They have not produced any results. They will produce no more results if they try it
out there than they will produce here. They have not invaded the field out there; they have not used their perfervid eloquence in taking up this question with the Progressive governments of Manitoba and Alberta, telling them where they were wrong and how they were trampling on the liberties of the people and infringing the sacred rights of democracy. No, hon. gentlemen will leave all that, come down to this parliament, and tell us that we are all going to the political bow-wows because we do not see just as the political group in that corner sees on this question.
I repeat what I said in the beginning. Having regard to the situation in the old country, to the development of democratic institutions there under the British system, because that is what he have had, the recognition of the rights of the people in that land where for centuries they have developed their institutions, and having regard at all times to the will of the people, I say that that is a very good and safe course for us to follow, and I for one believe that to depart from that course and to take away from the government of this country, whatever government it may be, the right to be guided according to what it believes to be the will of the people and, in any great crisis arising, to dissolve parliament and ascertain tfre will of the people, will be a retrograde step. I close by using again the sentence which I uttered in the beginning, namely, that I am glad on this occasion to take a few minutes in order to place myself in accord with the hon. gentleman for whom I have a great respect so far as his personality is concerned, but for whose politics I have very little use.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
I have said already that I am right notwithstanding. I think I may fairly repeat that the British system is the truly democratic system. Reference has been made to-night to those practices in the past in England when they had an aristrocratic government and corrupt boroughs. There was such a time in England and it took perhaps centuries for the people to get all their liberties, one after the other. They fought for those liberties; but there is no other system in the world

and I am proud to proclaim this to-night-which is as truly a popular and democratic system as the British one at present.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
Is the British system
finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSED VOTE OF HOUSE WHEN PRIOR TO EXPIRATION OF TERM
speechtext:
It is not finished; but
we must not go back; we must improve. I may remind my hon. friend that a change is not always a reform. There are changes which are retrograde and this would not be a reform. As regards the amendment, surely it cannot be expected that we should send a motion of this kind to a committee to amend or change the rules of the House. This is not a question of precedent; it is a question of principle, and personally I am not going to entrust any committee of my fellow members to decide my principles for me.

speechtext: I may be out of order, Mr. Speaker, but I was in my seat when the vote on the amendment was being taken, and I wish to record my vote for the amendment.

I think it should be recorded, because first of all, he was in his seat when the question was put, and Bourinot says at page 381:
If a member who has heard the question put does not vote, and the attention of the Speaker is directed to the fact, the latter will call upon him to declare on which side he votes: and his name will be recorded accordingly.
In the present instance, the hon. member was, as he says, in the House when the question was put. He had not made up his mind whether or not 'he would support the amendment when the vote on it was being taken, but later on, when the vote against the amendment was being taken, he made up his mind and stated that he wished to support the amendment. Under these circumstances I am justified in saying that his vote should be recorded. The question is now on the main motion.

I think there are very good grounds indeed, Mr. Speaker, why a resolution of this kind should not be referred to
the committee on the rules and practices of this House, but I think the subject, if there is time and an opportunity offers, is worthy of further consideration by this House, and as the hour is now l-ate, I would move the adjournment of the debate on the main motion.
